title: Shared Mutable State & Synchronization
scopeHtml: Scope: data races on multi-threaded dispatchers, @Volatile, atomics and StateFlow.update, Mutex (non-reentrant, vs synchronized), Semaphore, thread confinement, actor-style state, ConcurrentHashMap, plus scenarios (token-refresh race, double-tap submits, caches, bounded parallel uploads). Dispatcher internals live in C3, cancellation in C5, channels in C9, StateFlow mechanics in F2a.

notes.title: Why coroutines still have data races
notes.html:
The idea. A coroutine is not a thread. It is a piece of code that runs on threads. If two coroutines run on two threads at the same moment and both touch the same variable, you get exactly the same problems Java programmers have had since 1996. Coroutines make concurrency cheap to write, not safe by magic.

The mechanism. counter++ looks like one step but is three: read, add, write. On the JVM a top-level var compiles to roughly:

GETSTATIC counter     // read   -> 41
ICONST_1
IADD                  // add    -> 42
PUTSTATIC counter     // write  -> 42
Thread A (core 1)            Thread B (core 2)
read counter -> 41
                             read counter -> 41
add 1 -> 42
                             add 1 -> 42
write 42
                             write 42     <-- one increment lost

Dispatchers.Default is a pool with max(2, CPU cores) threads, so 100 coroutines doing counter++ 1,000 times really do run in parallel and the total is usually below 100,000. Inside a plain runBlocking, every coroutine runs on one thread in an event loop. counter++ has no suspension point, so no other coroutine can sneak in the middle. The result is exact. What matters is the number of threads the dispatcher uses, not whether you use coroutines.

var counter = 0
runBlocking(Dispatchers.Default) {
    repeat(100) { launch { repeat(1000) { counter++ } } }
}
println(counter) // e.g. 97 318

Real-world. A common production version: a repository keeps var cache: MutableMap or var unread = 0 and updates it from socket, push and database callbacks. In Crashlytics this shows up as ConcurrentModificationException (for plain HashMap/ArrayList), or as silent wrong numbers (badge counts that drift) that no stack trace explains. WhatsApp-style unread badges and Uber-style "trips today" counters have exactly this risk when several sources feed one counter.

Everyday analogy. Two cashiers update one paper ledger. Both read "balance 41", both write "42". One customer's payment simply vanishes. A single cashier (single thread) never has that problem.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "coroutines are lightweight so there are no races". Races depend on threads, not on coroutines.
  • Saying runBlocking is safe because it is "blocking". It is safe only because it is single-threaded, and it stops being safe the moment you pass Dispatchers.Default.
  • Forgetting that HashMap corruption (lost entries, even infinite loops on old JVMs) is worse than a lost increment.

notes.title: Volatile gives visibility, not atomicity
notes.html:
The idea. Each CPU core keeps its own fast copy (cache and registers) of memory. Without help, one thread may not see another thread's write for a while, or ever. @Volatile says: "always read and write this field straight from main memory, and make it visible to everyone".

The mechanism. @Volatile on a Kotlin property becomes the JVM volatile modifier. It guarantees two things: (1) visibility: a write is seen by later reads on other threads; (2) ordering: a happens-before edge, so everything done before the write is visible to a thread that reads the new value. It does not make counter++ atomic. The read-add-write is still three steps; volatile only makes each single read and write fresh.

@Volatile var counter = 0        // still loses increments
@Volatile var running = true     // good: one writer sets a flag, others read it

Good uses: a stop flag, a "config loaded" reference that is replaced as a whole (publish an immutable object), double-checked locking. Bad use: any read-modify-write (++, +=, "if null then set", check-then-act).

A coroutine that hops threads. Do you need @Volatile for a local var written before withContext(Dispatchers.IO) and read after? No. The coroutine machinery gives you a happens-before edge: everything before a suspension is visible after the resume, even on another thread, because the dispatcher hand-off (queue/lock inside the executor) publishes memory. Sequential code inside one coroutine behaves as if single-threaded. You only need protection when two coroutines at the same time share state, not when one coroutine moves between threads.

suspend fun load(): Int {
    var total = 0                          // plain local, no @Volatile
    total += 1
    withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { delay(10) }  // resumes maybe on another thread
    return total + 1                       // sees total == 1, guaranteed
}

Careful: if you capture that var in a parallel child (launch or async both writing it), that is shared state again, and you need a real tool.

Real-world. Google's own libraries use @Volatile for lazily published singletons (the classic Room INSTANCE pattern: @Volatile private var INSTANCE: AppDatabase? = null plus synchronized(this)). Kotlin's lazy default is SYNCHRONIZED for the same reason.

Everyday analogy. A noticeboard in the lobby. Volatile means everyone reads the real board, not their memory of it. It does not stop two people from erasing and rewriting the same number at the same time.

Common interview traps.

  • "Volatile makes count++ thread-safe". It does not.
  • Adding @Volatile to a mutable collection reference and thinking the contents are now safe.
  • Adding locks around a coroutine that merely switches threads. Unneeded.

notes.title: Atomics and compare-and-set
notes.html:
The idea. An atomic variable does the read-modify-write as one indivisible hardware step, with no lock. If someone else changed the value in between, it simply tries again.

The mechanism. AtomicInteger, AtomicLong, AtomicReference wrap a volatile field and use CPU instructions (LOCK CMPXCHG on x86, LDREX/STREX or LSE atomics on ARM) through VarHandle/Unsafe. The core is CAS (compare-and-set): "set to new only if the current value is still expected; tell me whether it worked".

val hits = AtomicInteger()
hits.incrementAndGet()                       // one atomic step

val ref = AtomicReference(State())
do {
    val old = ref.get()
    val new = old.copy(count = old.count + 1)
} while (!ref.compareAndSet(old, new))       // retry loop = what StateFlow.update does

Limits: atomics protect one variable. Two atomics changed together can still be seen half-updated; for that, put both inside one immutable object in an AtomicReference, or use a lock. CAS retry loops can spin under heavy contention, and the function you retry must be pure (it may run more than once). The ABA problem exists in theory (value goes A -> B -> A) but is harmless for immutable snapshots.

When to use in coroutine code: a counter, a "last seen id", an AtomicBoolean guard such as if (!started.compareAndSet(false, true)) return. These never suspend, so a plain atomic is cheaper and simpler than a Mutex.

Real-world. OkHttp's dispatcher counts running calls with atomics; Kotlin coroutines themselves use atomic state machines in Job, Channel and Mutex internals (kotlinx-atomicfu). Analytics SDKs use AtomicLong for event sequence numbers.

Everyday analogy. A ticket machine that hands out numbers. Each press gives a unique number in one motion. Nobody can get the same number twice.

Common interview traps.

  • Using two separate atomics and assuming they change together.
  • Doing slow or side-effecting work inside a CAS retry lambda (it can run several times).
  • Using atomics when the operation must suspend. You then need a Mutex or confinement.

notes.title: StateFlow update for atomic transitions
notes.html:
The idea. _state.value = _state.value.copy(x = 1) is read-modify-write again. Two coroutines can both read the old state and the later writer overwrites the earlier writer's change.

The mechanism. MutableStateFlow.update { } is a CAS loop:

// simplified from kotlinx.coroutines
inline fun <T> MutableStateFlow<T>.update(function: (T) -> T) {
    while (true) {
        val prev = value
        val next = function(prev)
        if (compareAndSet(prev, next)) return
    }
}

If another thread changed value between the read and the CAS, the lambda runs again with the fresh value. So the lambda must be pure and fast: no I/O, no Random, no incrementing counters outside. There is also updateAndGet and getAndUpdate. Note that compareAndSet uses equals, so equal states are conflated.

_state.update { it.copy(items = it.items + newItem) }   // safe from any thread
_state.update { it.copy(loading = false) }

update protects the transition of one StateFlow. If one logical change needs two StateFlows or a network call in the middle, put the whole thing in one state class, or guard the sequence with a Mutex.

Real-world. Google's architecture samples (NowInAndroid) and most MVI-style ViewModels use _uiState.update { } for this reason. A typical bug: a search ViewModel sets isLoading from a launch while another coroutine sets items; with .value = copy() the loading flag randomly sticks at true.

Everyday analogy. Editing a shared Google Doc where, if someone else saved first, the editor re-opens the new version and redoes your edit on top. Nobody's change is lost.

Common interview traps.

  • Putting side effects (analytics, list.add) inside the update lambda; it may execute twice.
  • Thinking .value = is atomic. The single write is, the read-copy-write sequence is not.
  • Mutating a list inside the state (it.items.add(x)) instead of copying: breaks equality and conflation.

notes.title: Mutex basics and reentrancy
notes.html:
The idea. A Mutex is a "one at a time" lock for coroutines. If it is taken, the next coroutine suspends (frees its thread) instead of blocking the thread.

The mechanism. kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Mutex: lock() and unlock() are the primitives; withLock { } is the safe wrapper (it unlocks in finally). It is fair: waiters resume in FIFO order. It is cancellable: a coroutine waiting in lock() that is cancelled just leaves the queue. Unlocking a mutex that is not locked throws IllegalStateException. There is tryLock(), isLocked, and an optional owner token.

private val mutex = Mutex()
private var balance = 0

suspend fun deposit(n: Int) = mutex.withLock {
    val b = balance
    delay(10)              // suspending inside is fine with Mutex
    balance = b + n
}

Non-reentrant. If a coroutine holds the mutex and calls another function that calls withLock on the same mutex, it waits for itself: a deadlock, with no exception, and the coroutine hangs forever (an ANR if on Main). Java's ReentrantLock and synchronized would let the owner in again; Mutex does not, because a coroutine has no stable thread identity and reentrancy would need to track the coroutine context.

suspend fun a() = mutex.withLock { b() }
suspend fun b() = mutex.withLock { /* never runs: deadlock */ }

Designs that avoid it: (1) public functions take the lock, private ...Locked() helpers assume the lock is held and never lock; (2) pass the "I already hold it" fact explicitly; (3) use a single-owner actor/confined dispatcher; (4) shrink the critical section so it calls nothing else.

Never hold a Mutex across slow I/O. One global Mutex around "check cache, fetch from network, store" serializes every caller behind the slowest request. At 10x traffic, the p99 latency becomes the sum of all queued requests, and a stuck request blocks everyone (a dead server turns into a frozen screen). Keep the lock only around the cheap in-memory part, or use per-key locking / deduplication (see the cache section below).

Real-world. Token refresh in OkHttp Authenticator implementations commonly uses a Mutex (or synchronized) so only one refresh happens (see the race section). Banking and trading apps (Zerodha Kite-style quote caches) keep their critical sections tiny.

Everyday analogy. One toilet key at a café. You hang up the key when done. If you ask the barista for the key while still holding it, you stand waiting for yourself forever.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming Mutex is reentrant like synchronized.
  • Calling lock() without try/finally (use withLock).
  • Holding the lock across api.call() or delay() without realizing the throughput cost.
  • Unlocking from a different owner/after the coroutine was cancelled without finally.

notes.title: Mutex vs synchronized
notes.html:
The idea. synchronized and ReentrantLock make the thread wait (block). Mutex makes the coroutine wait (suspend) and gives the thread back to other work.

Why suspend calls don't belong in synchronized. Kotlin forbids suspend calls inside a synchronized block (error: "The 'delay' suspension point is inside a critical section"). The reason: a suspended coroutine can resume on a different thread, and a monitor is owned by a thread, so unlocking from another thread would throw IllegalMonitorStateException (and meanwhile the first thread's monitor would be held while the coroutine is parked). ReentrantLock has the same thread-ownership problem; the compiler just doesn't warn for it.

synchronized / ReentrantLock Mutex
Waiting blocks the thread suspends the coroutine
Suspend calls inside forbidden / dangerous fine
Reentrant yes no
Cost when uncontended very cheap (biased/thin lock) an object plus atomics, a bit more
On Dispatchers.Main can freeze UI if held long safe
Fair no (ReentrantLock optional) FIFO

Rule of thumb: critical section is short, in-memory, non-suspending -> synchronized or an atomic (cheapest, and reentrant). Critical section must suspend (delay, withContext, channel, network) -> Mutex. Taking a blocking lock on Main while a background thread holds it for disk work is a classic ANR.

Real-world. Room, Glide and Coil use plain synchronized/ConcurrentHashMap for their internal caches because the sections never suspend. App-level repositories that fetch then store use Mutex.

Everyday analogy. synchronized is standing in the doorway doing nothing until the room frees up. Mutex is taking a number and sitting down; the waiter calls you when it is your turn.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming synchronized "works" with suspend functions because it compiles via a non-suspending lambda.
  • Using Mutex for a two-line in-memory update and paying overhead for nothing.
  • Blocking synchronized on the main thread against a background thread.

notes.title: Semaphore for bounded concurrency
notes.html:
The idea. A Mutex lets 1 in. A Semaphore lets N in. It is the right tool for "at most N things at once".

The mechanism. Semaphore(permits); acquire() suspends when no permits remain; release() gives one back; withPermit { } does both safely. Semaphore(1) behaves like a Mutex (but is not owner-tracked). Fair FIFO, cancellable.

val gate = Semaphore(4)
coroutineScope {
    photos.forEach { photo ->
        launch {                       // 2,000 coroutines are cheap (a few hundred bytes each)
            gate.withPermit { api.upload(photo) }   // only 4 uploads in flight
        }
    }
}

Why the unbounded version dies: photos.forEach { launch { upload(it) } } is cheap per coroutine, but each upload holds a decoded bitmap, an OkHttp request body, and sockets. 300 in flight on a 3 GB device means hundreds of MB and OOM. The semaphore limits resource use, not coroutine count. The semaphore must wrap the heavy part (decode and upload), not just the launch. Alternatives: Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(4) (limits threads, not suspended network waits, so it is less precise for async I/O), a fixed worker pool over a Channel, or Flow.flatMapMerge(concurrency = 4).

Real-world. Google Photos and Dropbox-style uploaders cap simultaneous uploads (often 2 to 4) and respect OkHttp's own maxRequestsPerHost (default 5). Coil and Glide limit decode threads similarly.

Everyday analogy. A bakery with 4 ovens. Customers queue; when an oven frees, the next tray goes in. You do not bake 2,000 trays at once.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing limitedParallelism(n) (threads running code) with a Semaphore (permits held across suspension).
  • Calling release() more than acquire() (throws IllegalStateException); always use withPermit.
  • Acquiring the permit after loading the big bitmap, defeating the purpose.

notes.title: Thread confinement with limitedParallelism
notes.html:
The idea. The best lock is no lock. If only one thread at a time ever touches the state, there is no race. Confinement means "all access goes through a single-threaded context".

Options compared.

Option What it is Notes
newSingleThreadContext("x") dedicates a real thread @DelicateCoroutinesApi, must close(), leaks a thread otherwise
Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher() same, you own the executor must close()
Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1) a view over the shared pool, max 1 running at a time no extra thread, nothing to close, since 1.6
Dispatchers.Main the UI thread already confined

Is limitedParallelism(1) really single-thread? It guarantees no two coroutines run concurrently on it, and consecutive tasks have happens-before ordering. It does not guarantee the same thread; tasks may hop across pool threads between runs. So ThreadLocal and thread-bound resources (a SQLite connection tied to a thread, Looper) need a real single thread. For plain shared state it is perfect.

private val confined = Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1)
private var cache = mutableMapOf<String, Article>()

suspend fun put(k: String, v: Article) = withContext(confined) { cache[k] = v }
suspend fun get(k: String) = withContext(confined) { cache[k] }

The catch: suspension points. Confinement stops parallel access, but a coroutine can suspend in the middle of a multi-step operation, and another coroutine on the same dispatcher then runs. Confinement protects each non-suspending chunk, not a whole suspend sequence (see the suspension-point section).

Migration with legacy callbacks. A Java SDK delivers onParticipantJoined/Left on 2 internal threads while new Kotlin code mutates the participant list. Fix: in the callback do no mutation; forward the event (scope.launch(confined) { apply(event) } or trySend into a channel) so that all reads and writes go through one context. Mixing "some code confined, some code touching the list from the callback thread" is worse than no design.

Real-world. The Android main thread is the original confinement model: every Compose state write and View update is expected there. Room runs transactions on a single transaction executor. Slack and WhatsApp-style sync engines usually confine their local store writes to one writer thread.

Everyday analogy. One person at the counter handles all orders in a shop. Customers queue but nobody argues over the till.

Common interview traps.

  • Using newSingleThreadContext and never closing it (leaked thread).
  • Believing limitedParallelism(1) means "same thread every time".
  • Assuming confinement makes read; suspend; write atomic. It does not.
  • limitedParallelism on Dispatchers.IO shares IO's 64-thread budget but is a separate view; it does not add threads.

notes.title: Actor style state ownership
notes.html:
The idea. Instead of many coroutines touching shared data, give the data to one coroutine (the owner) and let everyone else send it messages. Only the owner reads or writes; no locks needed.

The mechanism. A Channel of commands plus one consumer loop. Replies use a CompletableDeferred.

sealed interface Cmd
class Inc(val n: Int) : Cmd
class Get(val reply: CompletableDeferred<Int>) : Cmd

fun CoroutineScope.counterActor(): SendChannel<Cmd> {
    val ch = Channel<Cmd>(Channel.UNLIMITED)    // or a bounded buffer
    launch {
        var count = 0                           // owned by this coroutine only
        for (cmd in ch) when (cmd) {
            is Inc -> count += cmd.n
            is Get -> cmd.reply.complete(count)
        }
    }
    return ch
}

Messages are handled strictly one at a time and in order. The coroutine can safely suspend between messages; it can even suspend mid-handler since nobody else touches count.

Why actor {} is discouraged. The actor builder is marked @ObsoleteCoroutinesApi: it is tied to the older channel design and its exception/cancellation semantics are awkward (a crash closes the channel as "cancelled", callers see odd exceptions). A hand-rolled Channel plus launch, or produce, gives you explicit control of the buffer, error handling and shutdown. The pattern is great; the builder is not recommended.

Choosing a strategy (design question). Unread counter updated 200/s from 3 sources: AtomicInteger or MutableStateFlow.update. Draft map mutated by the UI: a ConcurrentHashMap is fine for single-key puts, or confine it. A sequence that must run read -> network -> write atomically per conversation: a per-key Mutex or an actor per conversation. Rule: pick the lightest tool that covers the atomic unit of your operation: single variable -> atomic; single-key map op -> concurrent map; multi-step in-memory -> confinement/Mutex; multi-step with suspension and ordering -> actor/Channel.

Real-world. Chat outboxes (WhatsApp, Telegram) process one queue per conversation to keep order. Redux/MVI "reducer loops" are actors: all intents go through one channel and are reduced sequentially.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant kitchen with one head chef who owns the pantry. Waiters hand in tickets; nobody else enters the pantry.

Common interview traps.

  • Using Channel.UNLIMITED with a slow consumer and growing memory without noticing.
  • Forgetting to close/cancel the actor when the owner scope ends.
  • Exposing the internal mutable state out of the actor (returning the live list instead of a copy).

notes.title: Concurrent collections and their limits
notes.html:
The idea. A thread-safe collection makes each single call safe. It does not make a sequence of calls safe.

The mechanism and limits.

  • ConcurrentHashMap: lock-striped/CAS buckets, safe put, get, remove, and atomic compound ops: putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent, compute, merge, replace. Does not allow null keys or values. Iterators are weakly consistent (no ConcurrentModificationException).
  • Still racy: check-then-act written by hand.
if (!map.containsKey(k)) map[k] = load(k)     // RACE: two threads both load
map.computeIfAbsent(k) { load(it) }           // atomic, but load() must be quick and non-suspending
  • computeIfAbsent runs its lambda while holding a bin lock, and cannot call a suspend function. For async per-key work, store a Deferred (or Lazy) in the map:
private val inFlight = ConcurrentHashMap<String, Deferred<Article>>()
suspend fun article(id: String): Article =
    inFlight.computeIfAbsent(id) { scope.async { api.load(id) } }.await()

Now 30 visible cards asking for the same ids make 30 requests, not 90, and everyone awaiting an id shares the result. Remember to remove the entry on completion/failure, otherwise failures are cached forever, and think about cancellation: if the first caller's scope created the async, cancelling that caller can cancel everyone, so use a longer-lived scope.

  • Collections.synchronizedList/Map: each method locked, but iteration and compound ops need a manual synchronized(list) { } block.
  • CopyOnWriteArrayList: every write copies the array; excellent for rarely-changed listener lists with many reads, terrible for frequent writes (O(n) per add, GC pressure).
  • Best of all: immutable snapshots in a StateFlow or AtomicReference.

Real-world. Coil/Glide memory caches, OkHttp connection pool, event bus subscriber lists (CopyOnWriteArrayList in EventBus-style libs) each choose according to read/write ratio.

Everyday analogy. A shop's single till is accurate, but "check shelf is empty then restock" by two staff at once may still order two boxes.

Common interview traps.

  • if (!map.containsKey) map.put is not atomic even on ConcurrentHashMap.
  • ConcurrentHashMap does not accept null values, so map[k] = null throws NPE.
  • Calling suspend code inside computeIfAbsent.
  • Using CopyOnWriteArrayList for a high-write buffer.

notes.title: Races at suspension points
notes.html:
The idea. Even on a single thread (Main), a coroutine can pause in the middle of a function, and another coroutine can run during the pause. A "check, suspend, act" sequence is therefore not atomic, even with no parallelism. This is a logical race, not a memory-visibility race.

Example. A balance check on Main:

suspend fun withdraw(amount: Int) {
    if (balance >= amount) {          // check
        api.authorize()               // suspends; another withdraw() runs now
        balance -= amount             // act: balance may now be negative
    }
}

Fixes: wrap the whole sequence in a Mutex (works on any dispatcher, including Main); or make the pause not matter (do check and update together in an update {}, then call the network and roll back on failure); or serialize via an actor.

Scenario: token refresh race. 1.2M DAU, 15-minute tokens. Five parallel API calls all get 401, and each starts a refresh. The server rotates the refresh token on every use, so refresh #1 succeeds, #2..#5 send the now-invalid old refresh token, get invalid_grant, and the app logs the user out (0.8% of sessions). Fix: a single-flight refresh: a Mutex (or shared Deferred) around "if the token is still the one that failed, refresh; otherwise reuse the newly refreshed token".

private val mutex = Mutex()
suspend fun refreshIfStale(failedToken: String): String = mutex.withLock {
    val current = store.token()
    if (current != failedToken) current          // someone else already refreshed
    else api.refresh(store.refreshToken()).also { store.save(it) }
}

Keep the I/O inside the lock here on purpose (the point is to serialize refreshes), but add a timeout.

Scenario: double-tap duplicate orders. Two taps 40 to 150 ms apart both launch POST /orders because the "disabled" flag is set after the first coroutine has started. Fixes in layers: ignore the second event synchronously (an AtomicBoolean.compareAndSet(false, true) or a state.update guard checked before launching), disable the button via state, and (the real safety net) send an idempotency key with the request so the server dedupes. Client-side guards reduce, only a server-side key eliminates, duplicates (retries, process restarts).

Real-world. Razorpay/Stripe style APIs have Idempotency-Key headers for exactly this. Swiggy/Zomato-type "Place order" buttons use a ViewModel guard plus server idempotency.

Everyday analogy. Two people each check "is the last seat free?", then both walk off to pay. Whoever pays second finds the seat taken. The check and the reservation must be one step.

Common interview traps.

  • "Main thread means no races". Interleaving at suspension points is still possible.
  • Disabling the button only through UI state that updates after a frame; a second tap can arrive first. Guard in the ViewModel.
  • Relying on client-side debouncing alone for payments.
  • Forgetting that the refresh Mutex must re-check the token inside the lock.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Races come from threads, not from coroutines. Dispatchers.Default is parallel; plain runBlocking is not.
  • @Volatile = visibility and ordering, never atomic read-modify-write. A coroutine hopping threads needs no extra protection.
  • One variable: atomics or StateFlow.update (pure lambda, CAS retry).
  • Needs to suspend inside the critical section: Mutex (non-reentrant, fair, never hold across slow I/O). Short non-suspending section: synchronized/atomics.
  • Semaphore = N permits, for bounded parallel work (uploads), wrapped around the heavy part.
  • Confinement: limitedParallelism(1) means one at a time, not one fixed thread, and does not make suspend sequences atomic.
  • Actor style: own state in one coroutine and talk via a Channel; prefer hand-rolled Channel to the obsolete actor {}.
  • Concurrent collections protect single calls only; cache Deferreds for per-key async dedup.
  • Main thread still has logical races at suspension points; use single-flight guards and idempotency keys for payments and token refresh.

questions.promptHtml: I launch 100 coroutines on Dispatchers.Default, and each one does counter++ 1,000 times. Why is the final value usually less than 100,000? Why does the same code give exactly 100,000 inside a plain runBlocking?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks whether you see coroutines as code running on threads, which brings back every JVM concurrency rule, rather than as some magic that makes races go away.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: counter++ isn't one operation. It's a read, an add and a write. Dispatchers.Default runs coroutines in parallel on a thread pool with one thread per CPU core (minimum 2). So two threads can read the same old value, both add one, and both write it back, and one increment is lost. Inside plain runBlocking, every coroutine runs on one thread through an event loop. counter++ has no suspension point, so no coroutine can get in the middle of it, and the result is exact. What matters is how many threads the dispatcher uses, not the fact that I'm using coroutines.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
On the JVM, counter++ on a top-level var compiles to roughly GETSTATIC counter; ICONST_1; IADD; PUTSTATIC counter. Those are three separate steps.

Thread A (core 1)            Thread B (core 2)
read counter  -> 41
                             read counter  -> 41
add 1         -> 42
                             add 1         -> 42
write 42
                             write 42        // one increment lost

Two problems combine here:

  1. Atomicity: the read-modify-write can interleave with another thread's.
  2. Visibility: with no happens-before edge, a thread may keep the value in a register or cache and never see the other thread's writes. The Java Memory Model only promises visibility through volatile, locks, atomics, thread start/join, and similar.

Why the single-thread case is exact: runBlocking (with no dispatcher argument) creates an event loop on the calling thread. Coroutines only switch at suspension points, and counter++ has none, so each increment finishes before another coroutine runs. The same holds for Dispatchers.Main. This doesn't mean "Main never needs care". Q440 covers races that happen at suspension points.

Dispatcher Threads counter++ race?
runBlocking event loop 1 No
Dispatchers.Main 1 (UI thread) No (no suspension inside ++)
Dispatchers.Default max(2, cores) Yes
Dispatchers.IO up to 64 (or cores, if more) Yes
limitedParallelism(1) view 1 at a time No

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun massiveRun(action: suspend () -> Unit) = coroutineScope {
    repeat(100) { launch { repeat(1_000) { action() } } }
}

var counter = 0

fun main() = runBlocking {
    withContext(Dispatchers.Default) {
        massiveRun { counter++ }        // BROKEN: parallel read-modify-write
    }
    println(counter)                    // e.g. 61_532, varies per run
}

// Fixed (simplest): an atomic
val atomicCounter = java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger()
// massiveRun { atomicCounter.incrementAndGet() }  -> always 100_000

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking that "coroutines are lightweight threads" means they're safe by default. On a pool dispatcher they are real parallel threads.
  • Testing on an emulator with 2 cores, seeing a correct result once, and calling it fixed. Races are probabilistic.
  • Adding @Volatile and expecting ++ to become atomic (see Q429).
  • Believing withContext(Dispatchers.Main) around the whole loop is free. It works, but now every increment has to hop to the UI thread.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Would the result be correct on a single-core device? → Default still has at least 2 threads, and the OS can preempt between the read and the write. So it's still racy, just rarer.
  2. Is counter += 1 any different? → No, it compiles to the same read-add-write.
  3. How do you prove a race exists in a test? → Run the operation many thousands of times on Dispatchers.Default with real threads (not a test dispatcher, which is single-threaded) and assert on the total. You can also use a stress-testing tool such as Lincheck. A runTest test won't reproduce it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "use synchronized". A senior explains that the race depends on the dispatcher's parallelism, separates atomicity from visibility, and lists the fix options (atomic, confinement, Mutex) with their costs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Analytics counters and "items downloaded" progress values updated from Dispatchers.IO workers commonly drift low, which shows up as stuck progress bars at 97%.

questions.promptHtml: What does @Volatile do in Kotlin, and why doesn't it fix the counter race?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: People confuse visibility with atomicity all the time. This question shows whether you know what the memory model actually guarantees.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: @Volatile (kotlin.concurrent.Volatile, or kotlin.jvm.Volatile on older versions) marks the JVM field as volatile. Every read then sees the latest write from any thread, and writes can't be reordered past it. That fixes visibility only. counter++ is still read, add, write, so two threads can read the same fresh value and both write the same result. Volatile is the right tool for one writer and many readers, like a stop flag or publishing an immutable snapshot. For read-modify-write I need an atomic, a lock, or confinement.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A volatile write happens-before every later volatile read of the same field. In practice that means:

  • no caching in a register across reads,
  • writes made before the volatile write (to any field) are visible to a thread that later reads the volatile field. That's the "safe publication" use.

It does not create a critical section. The interleaving diagram from Q428 is exactly the same with volatile. Both threads read 41, and that 41 was the freshest value at the time.

Where volatile is correct:

Pattern Volatile OK?
One thread writes a flag, others read it (@Volatile var running = true) Yes
Publishing a reference to an immutable object (@Volatile var config: Config) Yes
x++, x = x + 1, if (x == null) x = create() No, it's check-then-act or read-modify-write
Double-checked locking Yes, but only combined with a lock

Note on names: @Volatile has been available as kotlin.jvm.Volatile for a long time. Newer Kotlin versions (around 1.9/2.x) moved toward kotlin.concurrent.Volatile for multiplatform. Check your Kotlin version's stdlib docs. On the JVM both compile to the ACC_VOLATILE field flag.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Downloader {
    @Volatile private var cancelled = false        // OK: single writer, flag
    @Volatile private var done = 0                 // BROKEN for counting

    fun cancel() { cancelled = true }

    suspend fun run(files: List<String>) = coroutineScope {
        files.forEach { f ->
            launch(Dispatchers.IO) {
                if (cancelled) return@launch
                download(f)
                done++                              // still loses increments
            }
        }
    }
}

// Fix for the counter:
private val done = java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger()
// done.incrementAndGet()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• @Volatile var list = mutableListOf(). Only the reference is volatile. Mutating the list's contents from several threads is still a race.
  • Putting @Volatile on a val. It's pointless (and the compiler rejects it for vals), because final fields are already safely published after construction.
  • Using a volatile flag in place of coroutine cancellation. isActive / ensureActive() already exist (see C5).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does volatile cost anything? → Yes, a memory barrier on writes (and limits on reordering around reads). It's cheap compared with a lock, but not free in a hot loop.
  2. Why is by lazy safe without you writing volatile? → SynchronizedLazyImpl keeps its value in a @Volatile field and initializes it under synchronized. That's double-checked locking.
  3. Is a StateFlow.value read volatile-like? → In effect yes. StateFlow's state is updated under its internal synchronization and is safe to read from any thread. Read-modify-write through it is still not atomic unless you use update {} (Q435).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "volatile makes it thread-safe". A senior says "visibility, not atomicity", gives the single-writer / safe-publication use cases, and points out that only the reference is volatile.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A common bug is @Volatile var cache: MutableMap updated from IO workers. It "worked" until a ConcurrentModificationException showed up in Crashlytics, coming from a forEach on Main.

questions.promptHtml: How do AtomicInteger and AtomicReference work, and when are they the right tool in coroutine code?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Atomics are the cheapest correct fix for single-variable state. Interviewers want to see that you understand compare-and-set and its limits.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Atomics are built on a CPU compare-and-set instruction: "if the value is still X, replace it with Y, otherwise fail". incrementAndGet() loops on CAS until it wins, so no update is lost and no thread ever blocks. AtomicReference does the same for a reference. That's ideal for swapping a whole immutable snapshot (updateAndGet { it.copy(...) }). They work from any thread, never suspend, and are fine in coroutines. The limit is that they protect exactly one variable. As soon as an invariant spans two variables, or the update has to call a suspend function, I need a Mutex or confinement.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
CAS loop (what incrementAndGet / updateAndGet do):
loop:
  old = value              // volatile read
  new = f(old)             // pure computation
  if CAS(value, old, new)  // atomic in hardware
     return new
  else goto loop           // someone else won; retry with fresh value

Properties:

  • Lock-free: some thread always makes progress. There's no deadlock and nothing is held while a thread is descheduled.
  • The update function can run more than once under contention, so it must be pure. No logging, no analytics, no I/O.
  • ABA: CAS compares identity (for references) or the value (for ints). With immutable snapshots ABA is rarely a real problem. With pooled or mutable objects it can be.
  • Under heavy contention CAS loops spin and waste CPU. LongAdder (API 24+) spreads hot counters across cells.

Android notes: AtomicReference.updateAndGet/getAndUpdate and AtomicInteger.updateAndGet come from Java 8 and need API 24+. Below that, write the CAS loop yourself with compareAndSet. Kotlin also has kotlinx.atomicfu (common for KMP/library code), and recent Kotlin versions (2.1.20+) add experimental common atomics in kotlin.concurrent.atomics. Check the opt-in status for your version.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
data class Progress(val done: Int, val failed: Int)

class UploadTracker {
    private val progress = AtomicReference(Progress(0, 0))

    fun onSuccess() { progress.updateAndGet { it.copy(done = it.done + 1) } }   // API 24+
    fun onFailure() { progress.updateAndGet { it.copy(failed = it.failed + 1) } }
    fun snapshot(): Progress = progress.get()
}

// BROKEN: two separate atomics can't keep an invariant between them
val done = AtomicInteger(); val total = AtomicInteger()
fun percent() = done.get() * 100 / total.get()   // reads may come from different moments

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Side effects inside updateAndGet { }, which then fire twice under contention.
  • if (ref.get() == null) ref.set(create()). That's check-then-act; use compareAndSet(null, create()).
  • Holding a mutable object in AtomicReference and mutating it. The atomicity only covers swapping the reference.
  • Trying to call a suspend function in the lambda. It's a Java UnaryOperator, not inline, so it doesn't compile.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Atomic vs synchronized for a counter? → Atomic: lock-free and cheaper under low and moderate contention. synchronized is needed when several fields must change together.
  2. What's LongAdder for? → High-contention counters that you rarely read. Writes go to per-thread cells and sum() adds them up.
  3. Why does MutableStateFlow.update {} look exactly like updateAndGet? → It is the same CAS loop over compareAndSet (Q435). It just also notifies collectors.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "AtomicInteger is thread-safe". A senior explains the CAS retry loop, the purity requirement, the one-variable limit, and the API-level and contention caveats.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Download managers often keep AtomicReference<Map<Id, Progress>> snapshots so the UI thread can read a consistent map without locks while the IO workers swap in new copies.

questions.promptHtml: What is kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Mutex, how do you use it, and how is it different from a Java lock?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's the coroutine-native lock. They want to hear "suspends instead of blocking" and see withLock used correctly.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Mutex is a coroutine lock with two states, locked and unlocked. lock() is a suspend function. If the mutex is taken, the coroutine suspends and frees its thread, instead of blocking the thread like synchronized does. I nearly always use mutex.withLock { }, which does lock, try, and finally-unlock. Because it suspends, the critical section can contain suspend calls. That's the reason to choose it over synchronized. It's fair (waiters get the lock in FIFO order) and it is not reentrant.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
API surface (kotlinx.coroutines 1.x):

Member Meaning
suspend fun lock(owner: Any? = null) Suspends until acquired. Cancellable while waiting.
fun tryLock(owner: Any? = null): Boolean Non-suspending attempt
fun unlock(owner: Any? = null) Releases. Throws IllegalStateException if not locked (or the owner doesn't match).
val isLocked Snapshot only, so don't branch on it for correctness
fun holdsLock(owner: Any): Boolean Debugging aid
suspend inline fun <T> Mutex.withLock(owner, action: () -> T): T The idiom you should use

Runtime behavior:

  • A waiting coroutine sits in the mutex's queue. Its thread goes back to the dispatcher and runs other work, so 1,000 waiters cost 1,000 small objects, not 1,000 blocked threads.
  • No thread affinity: you can lock on Dispatchers.IO thread #3 and unlock after resuming on thread #7. A ReentrantLock would throw IllegalMonitorStateException in that case.
  • Cancellation while waiting: the coroutine gets CancellationException and doesn't acquire the lock. Cancellation inside withLock still unlocks, thanks to the finally.
  • Cost: each contended lock is a suspend plus resume through the dispatcher. That's much more expensive than a CAS. The official kotlinlang "Shared mutable state" guide shows a fine-grained withLock { counter++ } running noticeably slower than coarser approaches.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class SessionRepository(private val api: AuthApi, private val store: TokenStore) {
    private val mutex = Mutex()
    private var cachedProfile: Profile? = null

    suspend fun profile(): Profile = mutex.withLock {
        cachedProfile ?: api.fetchProfile().also { cachedProfile = it }   // suspend call inside: OK
    }
}

// BROKEN: manual lock without finally; an exception leaves it locked forever
suspend fun bad(m: Mutex) {
    m.lock()
    riskyCall()          // throws -> unlock never runs -> every later caller hangs
    m.unlock()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Manual lock()/unlock() without try/finally.
  • Locking a whole repository around network I/O, which serializes every request (see Q446).
  • Expecting reentrancy (Q434).
  • Creating the Mutex() inside the function. Each call gets a new lock, so it protects nothing.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is Mutex fair? → Yes. The docs describe it as granting the lock in first-come, first-served order.
  2. Does withLock work from Java? → No, it's a suspend inline function. Java callers need another mechanism (see Q447).
  3. Can a Mutex protect state shared with non-coroutine Java threads? → Only if those threads also go through the Mutex, which means runBlocking or tryLock. In mixed worlds a non-suspending primitive (atomic/synchronized) is usually cleaner.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "a lock for coroutines". A senior adds suspend-not-block, no thread affinity, cancellation semantics, fairness, cost compared with atomics, and why isLocked must not be used for decisions.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that swapped synchronized for Mutex everywhere in one sweep have seen latency regressions in hot paths that never suspended in the first place. Mutex pays off only when the critical section suspends.

questions.subtopic: Visibility when one coroutine hops threads
questions.promptHtml: A coroutine writes a local var on one thread, then resumes on a different thread after withContext or delay. Do I need @Volatile or a lock for that variable?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It shows whether you understand where kotlinx.coroutines already provides happens-before guarantees, and where it doesn't.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: No. A single coroutine runs sequentially even when it hops threads. The library guarantees that everything before a suspension happens-before the code after resumption, because the hand-off goes through the dispatcher's queue and executor, and those include memory barriers. So locals and spilled state machine fields are always visible to the resumed code. What I do need to protect is state that two coroutines touch at the same time: a field on a class, a shared map, a global. The rule is about concurrent access, not about thread switches.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
When a coroutine suspends, its locals are "spilled" into fields of the continuation object (see C1a). On resume, a dispatcher thread calls resumeWith. The hand-off path is "continuation enqueued into the dispatcher's task queue → worker thread dequeues it". It relies on concurrent queues and atomic operations, and those establish a happens-before edge between the enqueue and the dequeue.

Thread A                          Thread B
x = 5 (spilled to continuation)
suspend -> enqueue(task) ───HB───▶ dequeue(task)
                                  resume: reads x == 5  (guaranteed)

Two different coroutines get no such ordering between them, because nothing synchronizes them:

coroutine 1 on Default-1: this.items.add(a)
coroutine 2 on Default-2: this.items.add(b)    // concurrent -> race

Rules I state in reviews:

  1. Locals in one coroutine are safe. A coroutine is sequential.
  2. Children launched with launch/async that write to the parent's captured var run concurrently. That's a race.
  3. join()/await() do create happens-before: the child's writes are visible after await returns. So "launch, write a field, join, read the field" is correct, but reading the field while the child is still running isn't.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun loadAll(): Int {
    var total = 0                                  // local
    total += withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { db.count() }
    delay(100)                                     // may resume on another thread
    total += withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { api.count() }
    return total                                   // correct, no volatile needed
}

suspend fun broken(ids: List<Int>): Int = coroutineScope {
    var sum = 0
    ids.forEach { id -> launch(Dispatchers.Default) { sum += compute(id) } }  // children race on captured var
    sum                                            // also read before children finish!
}

suspend fun fixed(ids: List<Int>): Int = coroutineScope {
    ids.map { id -> async(Dispatchers.Default) { compute(id) } }.awaitAll().sum()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Adding @Volatile everywhere "because coroutines switch threads". It's noise that hides the real shared state.
  • Sharing a captured var across launch children (it compiles to a Ref.IntRef that is shared by all of them).
  • Reading results before join/await. That's a visibility bug and a logic bug.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is this guarantee documented? → The coroutines docs say a coroutine is sequential, and the dispatchers are built on executors and queues that give the JMM ordering. I'd describe it as a library guarantee, not a language one.
  2. Does Dispatchers.Unconfined keep the guarantee? → Yes for one coroutine. Resumption still happens through a resumeWith call on whatever thread completed the suspension. The usual Unconfined pitfalls are about which thread, not visibility.
  3. What about a ThreadLocal read after the hop? → Different thread, different value, unless you use asContextElement (see C1b).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer either says "add volatile to be safe" or "coroutines are single-threaded". A senior separates intra-coroutine sequencing from inter-coroutine concurrency and names join/await as synchronization points.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Code reviews often catch var result captured and mutated by several launch blocks in a coroutineScope. It passed unit tests with a single-threaded test dispatcher and failed on real devices.

questions.promptHtml: When would you use Mutex and when synchronized (or ReentrantLock) in coroutine code? Why can't you just call suspend functions inside synchronized?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Picking the wrong primitive causes either thread starvation or needless overhead. This is a judgment question.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: synchronized is tied to a thread. The monitor belongs to the thread that entered it, and the thread blocks while it waits. A suspension inside the block would let the coroutine resume on another thread while the original thread still owns the monitor, so Kotlin rejects a suspend call inside synchronized {} at compile time ("suspension point is inside a critical section"). My rule: if the critical section is short, CPU-only and never suspends, synchronized or an atomic is cheaper and works from Java too. If the critical section must suspend, like a network call, a DB call or delay, I use Mutex, which suspends waiters instead of blocking threads.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Aspect synchronized / ReentrantLock Mutex
Waiting Blocks the OS thread Suspends the coroutine; thread is freed
Ownership Thread Optional owner token, no thread affinity
Reentrant Yes No
Suspend inside Compile error with synchronized{}; ReentrantLock compiles but is broken Allowed
Java callers Yes No (suspend API)
Uncontended cost Very low (biased/thin locks) Higher (object + state machine)
Contended cost Blocked thread; can starve the 64-thread IO pool or the core-sized Default pool Suspend/resume dispatch

Why ReentrantLock + suspend is worse than a compile error: lock.lock(); delay(10); lock.unlock() compiles. After delay, the coroutine can resume on another thread and unlock() throws IllegalMonitorStateException. Or it resumes on the same thread and another coroutine on that thread re-enters the lock, because it's reentrant per thread. That silently breaks mutual exclusion. C1b covers this case in its scenario. Here the point is the selection rule.

Blocking on a pool dispatcher: if 8 coroutines on an 8-thread Default all block on synchronized while the holder waits on something that also needs Default, the pool is starved and the app stalls.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Good: tiny CPU-only section, callable from Java too
private val lock = Any()
private val lru = LinkedHashMap<String, Bitmap>(16, 0.75f, true)
fun getBitmap(key: String): Bitmap? = synchronized(lock) { lru[key] }

// Good: section must suspend
private val mutex = Mutex()
suspend fun refreshIfStale() = mutex.withLock {
    if (isStale()) save(api.fetch())           // suspend calls under lock
}

// Doesn't compile: suspension point inside critical section
// synchronized(lock) { api.fetch() }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrapping runBlocking inside synchronized to "make it work". That blocks a thread for the whole network call.
  • Using ReentrantLock across withContext. It compiles and fails at runtime.
  • Switching all synchronized to Mutex for style. That's slower for non-suspending sections and loses Java interop.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can I do synchronized work in a coroutine at all? → Yes, as long as the block doesn't suspend. It briefly blocks the thread like any other short computation.
  2. What about ReadWriteLock semantics? → There's no coroutine read/write mutex in the stable API. Use an immutable snapshot (StateFlow/AtomicReference) for reads and serialize the writes.
  3. Does a blocked synchronized waiter respond to coroutine cancellation? → No. Blocking isn't cancellable; only suspending is.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "Mutex for coroutines, synchronized for threads". A senior bases the choice on whether the section suspends, mentions the compile-time check and the ReentrantLock loophole, and weighs Java interop and cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Room-backed repository where the team moved the synchronized cache around withContext(Dispatchers.IO) to ReentrantLock "to fix the compile error" ended up with intermittent IllegalMonitorStateException in production.

questions.promptHtml: Mutex isn't reentrant. What happens when a coroutine that holds the lock calls a function that tries to take the same lock, and how do you design around that?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Self-deadlock with Mutex is a classic production hang. This checks whether you know both the symptom and the structural fix.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The second lock() suspends forever. The mutex is held, and the only coroutine that could release it is the one now waiting. There's no exception and no ANR, because nothing is blocked; the coroutine just never resumes, and the screen spins forever. If I pass an owner token, the second lock with the same owner throws IllegalStateException instead, which at least fails fast. The real fix is structural: lock only at the public entry points, and have them call private *Locked helpers that assume the lock is already held and never take it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Why no reentrancy: a reentrant lock needs an identity for "the same holder". For synchronized that's the thread. A coroutine has no stable thread, and treating "the same Job" as the owner breaks down as soon as you launch a child that needs the lock. kotlinx.coroutines chose simplicity: no reentrancy, plus an optional explicit owner.

withLock (held by C1)
   └── save()  -> mutex.withLock  // C1 suspends waiting for itself
                                  // C1 never resumes -> deadlock
                                  // all other callers also queue forever

Indirect reentrancy is the dangerous kind:

  • holding the lock while emitting into a flow whose collector calls back into the same repository,
  • holding the lock while invoking a listener or callback supplied by the caller,
  • holding the lock and calling async { } where the child needs the lock, then await (child waits for the parent, parent waits for the child).

Diagnosis: DebugProbes.dumpCoroutines() (kotlinx-coroutines-debug) shows the coroutine SUSPENDED inside MutexImpl.lock, with the caller holding the lock in its stack. mutex.holdsLock(owner) can back an assertion in debug builds.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class CartRepository(private val dao: CartDao) {
    private val mutex = Mutex()

    // BROKEN
    suspend fun addItem(item: Item) = mutex.withLock {
        dao.insert(item)
        recalcTotals()                  // takes the same mutex -> hangs forever
    }
    suspend fun recalcTotals() = mutex.withLock { dao.updateTotals(dao.sum()) }

    // FIXED: public entry points lock, private helpers assume the lock is held
    suspend fun addItemFixed(item: Item) = mutex.withLock {
        dao.insert(item)
        recalcTotalsLocked()
    }
    suspend fun recalcTotalsPublic() = mutex.withLock { recalcTotalsLocked() }
    private suspend fun recalcTotalsLocked() { dao.updateTotals(dao.sum()) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling external code (listeners, flow emissions, user lambdas) while holding the lock.
  • "Fixing" the hang with tryLock() and skipping the work when it fails. That turns a hang into silently dropped updates.
  • Wrapping withTimeout around the lock to "detect" the deadlock in production and then retrying. The lock is still held.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Could I build a reentrant mutex with a context element? → It's possible (store the owner in the CoroutineContext), but children and async get it wrong easily. I'd restructure the code instead.
  2. Does the Mutex's FIFO fairness matter here? → No. The holder is waiting on itself, so the queue order doesn't help.
  3. How do you catch this in tests? → Use runTest with a timeout. A self-deadlock shows up as a test that hangs, and runTest's default timeout (60 s in recent 1.7+ versions; verify for your version) fails it with a coroutine dump.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "it deadlocks". A senior explains why there's no ANR, shows the owner fail-fast option, the "locked helper" pattern and the rule against calling foreign code under a lock, and knows how to diagnose it with DebugProbes.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A sync engine that held its Mutex while emitting progress into a MutableSharedFlow hung whenever the UI's collector triggered a "retry now" call into the same engine. Users saw an endless spinner and Crashlytics recorded no crashes.

questions.promptHtml: Why is _state.value = _state.value.copy(...) unsafe from multiple coroutines, and how does MutableStateFlow.update {} fix it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's the most common real-world race in ViewModels. It tests whether you see .value read plus .value write as two operations.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: _state.value = _state.value.copy(x = 1) reads, computes and writes in three steps. If another coroutine on another thread does the same with a different field, one of the writes overwrites the other with a stale copy and an update is lost. update { it.copy(x = 1) } runs a compare-and-set loop: read the current value, run my lambda, and compareAndSet(old, new). If someone changed the value in between, it re-runs the lambda on the fresh value. So no update is lost. The lambda must be pure because it can run more than once. If the update needs a suspend call, I do that first and then apply only the cheap state change inside update.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
MutableStateFlow is thread-safe for each single .value read or write. That doesn't make a sequence of them atomic.

value = A(loading=true, items=[])
C1 (IO-1): reads A      C2 (IO-2): reads A
C1: copy(items=[x]) -> B   C2: copy(loading=false) -> C
C1: value = B              C2: value = C      // C has items=[] : C1's update lost

update is defined as (simplified):

inline fun <T> MutableStateFlow<T>.update(function: (T) -> T) {
    while (true) {
        val prevValue = value
        val nextValue = function(prevValue)
        if (compareAndSet(prevValue, nextValue)) return
    }
}

updateAndGet and getAndUpdate are the same loop with a different return value. They were added in kotlinx.coroutines 1.5.1 or so; check your version if you're on an old library. Details worth knowing:

  • compareAndSet uses equality (==) on the value, the same way StateFlow's conflation does. If the lambda returns an equal value, nothing is emitted.
  • The lambda can run more than once, so no side effects (no logging an event, no sending analytics, no launch).
  • Assigning .value is still fine when there is one writer, or when the new value doesn't depend on the old one (_state.value = State.Loading from a single place).
  • update doesn't help you coordinate with other state. If the transition depends on both StateFlow A and StateFlow B, you need confinement or a Mutex around both (or fold both into one state object).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
data class CartState(val items: List<Item> = emptyList(), val loading: Boolean = false, val total: Long = 0)

class CartViewModel(private val repo: CartRepository) : ViewModel() {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow(CartState())
    val state: StateFlow<CartState> = _state.asStateFlow()

    fun add(item: Item) = viewModelScope.launch(Dispatchers.Default) {
        _state.value = _state.value.copy(items = _state.value.items + item)   // BROKEN under concurrency
    }

    fun addSafe(item: Item) = viewModelScope.launch(Dispatchers.Default) {
        _state.update { it.copy(items = it.items + item, total = it.total + item.price) }   // atomic
    }

    fun refresh() = viewModelScope.launch {
        _state.update { it.copy(loading = true) }
        val fresh = repo.load()                       // suspend work OUTSIDE update
        _state.update { it.copy(items = fresh, loading = false) }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Doing repo.load() or Log/analytics inside update {}. The lambda is not suspend, and side effects repeat on retry.
  • Believing everything is safe because the ViewModel runs on Main. The moment someone writes launch(Dispatchers.IO) { _state.value = ... } the race exists.
  • Computing the new state from a separate earlier read (val s = _state.value; ...; _state.value = s.copy()). Same race, just spread out.
  • Mutating a MutableList inside the state. Then there's no new value to compare, so nothing is emitted (that's the F2b chunk's scenario).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not make _state a Mutex-guarded var instead? → update is lock-free and cheaper, and the state is already published through the flow. Use a Mutex only if the transition itself must suspend.
  2. Does update guarantee collectors see each intermediate value? → No. StateFlow conflates, so a slow collector may skip states. Nothing is lost from the state, only from the observed history.
  3. Two ViewModel functions both call update. Is order guaranteed? → The updates are linearizable (each applies on top of the previous), but the interleaving is whichever CAS wins. If order matters, serialize the producers (Q437/Q438).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "use update because it's thread-safe". A senior shows the lost-update interleaving, states that the lambda must be pure because of retries, keeps suspend work outside it, and notes that a transition spanning several flows needs something stronger.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: In a checkout screen, the shipping, coupon and totals handlers each did _state.value = _state.value.copy(...) from different dispatchers. QA saw coupons that "disappeared" about 1 in 200 times. Replacing them with update made the issue go away.

questions.promptHtml: What does kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore do, how is it different from Mutex, and when do you use it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Limiting concurrency (uploads, API calls, decode jobs) is everyday senior work. They want a correct, cancellation-safe tool and not an ad-hoc counter.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Semaphore(permits) allows at most N coroutines inside a section at once. acquire() takes a permit or suspends, and release() returns it. withPermit { } does both with try/finally. A Mutex is basically a semaphore with 1 permit, but Mutex is for protecting state (exclusion), while a semaphore is for limiting throughput (a resource cap, like 3 parallel uploads). It's fair and FIFO, it suspends instead of blocking, and over-releasing throws IllegalStateException. Important: it caps how many are in flight, but it does not cap how many coroutines I create. For 100k items I still shouldn't launch 100k coroutines.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
API (from the official docs): availablePermits, suspend acquire(), release(), tryAcquire(), and the withPermit {} extension. Properties:

  • FIFO fairness: the longest-waiting acquirer gets the next permit.
  • Cancellation: a coroutine suspended in acquire() that is cancelled does not take a permit. The one inside withPermit releases on exit even when cancelled.
  • Not reentrant, no owner: a nested withPermit in the same coroutine takes a second permit. With Semaphore(1), that self-deadlocks just like Mutex.
  • Over-release: release() more than acquire() throws IllegalStateException. This is why raw acquire/release in different code paths is risky.

Semaphore vs the other ways to cap concurrency:

Tool What it caps Notes
Semaphore(n) Coroutines inside a section Any dispatcher, any suspend code inside
Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(n) Threads running tasks Only limits threads executing code, not suspended coroutines; a suspended coroutine doesn't count
flatMapMerge(concurrency = n) Concurrent inner flows Natural for Flow pipelines (F3 chunk)
Worker pool of n consumers on a Channel Concurrent consumers Also bounds the coroutine count (C9 chunk)

Because a coroutine suspended in delay or a network call holds its permit but no thread, limitedParallelism(n) would NOT cap in-flight network calls, but a semaphore does.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
private val uploadPermits = Semaphore(permits = 3)

suspend fun uploadAll(files: List<File>): List<UploadResult> = coroutineScope {
    files.map { f ->
        async {                                   // creates N coroutines, but only 3 run the body
            uploadPermits.withPermit { api.upload(f) }
        }
    }.awaitAll()
}

// BROKEN: manual pairing, permit leaks on exception
suspend fun leaky(f: File) {
    uploadPermits.acquire()
    api.upload(f)                                 // throws -> release never runs; after 3 failures everything hangs
    uploadPermits.release()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Raw acquire()/release() without finally. Permits leak and the app slowly freezes.
  • Using limitedParallelism(3) to cap network calls and wondering why 50 were in flight.
  • Creating the Semaphore per call. It then limits nothing. Make it a field with the right lifetime.
  • Launching 100k coroutines that all queue on the semaphore. It works but wastes memory; use a worker pool or flatMapMerge.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you pick N? → From the bottleneck: OkHttp's default Dispatcher.maxRequestsPerHost is 5, so more than that just queues in OkHttp; on mobile radios 3-6 parallel uploads is typical. Measure.
  2. Is there a Flow equivalent? → flatMapMerge(concurrency = n) or buffer-based worker patterns.
  3. Semaphore with 0 permits? → Useful as a signal/gate (acquire suspends until another coroutine releases). A CompletableDeferred or Channel usually reads clearer.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "like a Mutex with N permits". A senior contrasts it with limitedParallelism (threads vs in-flight coroutines), mentions fairness and leak-safety through withPermit, and notes that a semaphore doesn't bound the number of coroutines.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An image-sync feature used launch per photo with no cap. Users with 2,000 photos saw OOM and a 429 storm. A Semaphore(3) plus lazy iteration fixed both.

questions.promptHtml: Explain thread confinement as a way to avoid locks in coroutines. What's the difference between newSingleThreadContext, an executor dispatcher and Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1), and is limitedParallelism(1) a mutex?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Confinement is the idiomatic alternative to locks, but people misunderstand what limitedParallelism(1) guarantees. The "it's not a mutex" point separates juniors from seniors.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Confinement means that all access to a piece of state happens on one thread (or one at a time), so no lock is needed. I give the state an owner and run all access through a dispatcher with parallelism 1. The modern way is Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1) (or Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(1) if the code blocks). It's a view over the shared pool, needs no closing and doesn't permanently take a thread. newSingleThreadContext or Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher() create a real dedicated thread that I must close(). The key point: limitedParallelism(1) limits threads, not coroutines. Code is sequential between suspension points, but if a coroutine suspends in the middle, another coroutine on that view can start. So it protects counter++, but not a "read, call suspend, write" sequence. For that sequence I need a Mutex.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Dispatchers.Default (N threads)
   └── view: limitedParallelism(1)   // at most one task runs at a time; may be a different thread each time
Option Real thread? Cleanup Same thread always? Notes
newSingleThreadContext("name") Yes, dedicated close(), or it leaks a thread Yes Marked @DelicateCoroutinesApi; in Android prefer a view
Executor.asCoroutineDispatcher() Whatever the executor is Must shutdown the executor (or close() the dispatcher) If single-thread executor Good when a Java library hands you an executor
Default.limitedParallelism(1) No, borrowed None No, may hop across pool threads Happens-before between consecutive tasks is guaranteed (per the docs)
Dispatchers.Main Yes n/a Yes Already confined; Main.limitedParallelism(1) returns Main

Guarantee: with a parallelism-1 view, the code between two suspension points runs exclusively, and consecutive tasks have a happens-before relation. That is enough for plain var state without @Volatile, as long as the only access is from that view.

What it does not give: atomicity across suspension points.

view(1):  C1: read x=0 ── suspend (await net) ─────────────── write x=1
          C2:            run: read x=0 ── suspend ── write x=1   // both read 0: lost update

limitedParallelism is available since kotlinx.coroutines 1.6.0 as experimental and has been stable since 1.9.0, so on older versions you may need the opt-in annotation. Verify against your project's version. On Dispatchers.IO, views are elastic: their parallelism isn't capped by IO's 64-thread limit, so a view with limitedParallelism(100) can use 100 threads.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class InMemoryStore {
    private val confined = Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1, "store")
    private val map = HashMap<String, Item>()            // plain HashMap: only touched on `confined`

    suspend fun put(k: String, v: Item) = withContext(confined) { map[k] = v }
    suspend fun get(k: String): Item? = withContext(confined) { map[k] }

    // BROKEN: check-then-act across a suspension; limitedParallelism(1) is not a mutex
    suspend fun getOrFetch(k: String): Item = withContext(confined) {
        map[k] ?: api.fetch(k).also { map[k] = it }      // two coroutines can both miss and both fetch
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• newSingleThreadContext in an Application field and never closed, or created per call (a thread leak per call).
  • Thinking limitedParallelism(1) gives mutual exclusion across suspend calls.
  • Accessing the state "just for reading" from another dispatcher. One stray access ends the safety.
  • Confining on Dispatchers.Main for heavy state and adding jank.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is coarse confinement faster than fine-grained? → The official guide's example: wrapping each counter++ in withContext(single) pays a dispatch per increment, while moving the whole loop into the single-thread context pays once. Cost is in the context switches.
  2. Do I need @Volatile on state confined to the view? → No, the view's sequential tasks have happens-before.
  3. Can the view starve? → Yes. If a task blocks the one slot (blocking I/O or Thread.sleep), everything queued behind it waits.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "single thread dispatcher so no locks". A senior says limitedParallelism(1) is a view over a shared pool, not a mutex, gives the suspension-point caveat, and adds lifecycle, cleanup and version notes.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team confined an in-memory cache to limitedParallelism(1) and still got duplicate network fetches, because the miss check and the fetch were separated by a suspension. They added a per-key Deferred map (Q443).

questions.promptHtml: What is the actor pattern for shared state in coroutines? Show how you'd build a safe counter or cache as an "actor", and why the old actor {} builder isn't the recommended way anymore.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you can design state ownership (one owner, messages in) instead of sprinkling locks, and whether you know the status of the actor API.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An actor is a coroutine that owns some state, plus a channel of messages. Everyone else sends messages. Only the actor's coroutine reads or writes the state, so there is no sharing and no lock. Because it processes one message at a time, operations are naturally serialized, and it can hold suspend calls in its handler. The actor {} builder is marked @ObsoleteCoroutinesApi; the docs say it will be replaced by a more flexible design with more complex rules, so I build the same thing by hand: a Channel of a sealed interface Msg, a loop in a scope I own, and CompletableDeferred for replies. I accept the cost: serialization means one slow message delays everything behind it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
callers (any thread)                    actor coroutine (single consumer)
  send(Inc)  ─┐                           for (msg in channel) {
  send(Add)  ─┼──▶ Channel<Msg> ──────▶     when (msg) { ... mutate private state ... }
  send(Get(reply)) ─┘                         reply.complete(value)
                                          }

Design rules:

  1. State is private to the loop function, never exposed. Replies are immutable snapshots.
  2. Request/response uses CompletableDeferred<T> carried in the message.
  3. Channel capacity decides backpressure: UNLIMITED never suspends senders (memory risk), BUFFERED/rendezvous suspend them. Choose consciously (C9 owns the channel details).
  4. The loop must handle CancellationException properly and complete pending replies on shutdown, or callers wait forever. I use try/finally to cancel or fail outstanding deferreds.
  5. Exceptions in a handler kill the actor if unhandled; one bad message shouldn't kill the loop, so catch per message (rethrow CancellationException) and fail that message's reply.

Actor vs Mutex vs StateFlow.update:

Actor Mutex update {}
Serialization Strict FIFO message order FIFO lock order None (CAS retry)
Suspend inside handler Yes Yes No
Boilerplate High Low Lowest
Failure isolation Per-message handling try/finally n/a
Best for Complex state machines, ordering matters, many operations A few critical sections Single-value state

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
sealed interface CounterMsg {
    data class Add(val n: Int) : CounterMsg
    data class Get(val reply: CompletableDeferred<Int>) : CounterMsg
}

class CounterActor(scope: CoroutineScope) {
    private val inbox = Channel<CounterMsg>(Channel.UNLIMITED)

    init {
        scope.launch {
            var count = 0                                    // owned by this coroutine only
            try {
                for (msg in inbox) when (msg) {
                    is CounterMsg.Add -> count += msg.n
                    is CounterMsg.Get -> msg.reply.complete(count)
                }
            } finally {
                inbox.close()                                // reject new sends after shutdown
            }
        }
    }

    fun add(n: Int) { inbox.trySend(CounterMsg.Add(n)) }     // fire-and-forget
    suspend fun get(): Int = CompletableDeferred<Int>().also { inbox.send(CounterMsg.Get(it)) }.await()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Returning a mutable collection from Get, which leaks the confined state.
  • Forgetting to complete pending Get replies on shutdown, so callers hang.
  • Doing a slow network call in the handler and then wondering why every other message is delayed.
  • Using the actor for a single counter where AtomicInteger is two lines.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not use the actor {} builder? → It still works but carries @ObsoleteCoroutinesApi. The hand-rolled channel and loop is the same thing, with explicit control over lifecycle and failure.
  2. How do you avoid unbounded growth of UNLIMITED? → Bound the channel and decide between suspend, DROP_OLDEST or fail. Or coalesce messages.
  3. How is it different from the MVI reducer pattern? → An MVI reducer consuming intents from a channel is an actor. The state is the confined value, and published copies go out through StateFlow.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "an actor serializes access". A senior builds it with sealed messages and CompletableDeferred, handles shutdown and error per message, knows the builder's obsolete status, and weighs it against Mutex and update.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A sync engine whose state (queue, in-flight set, backoff timers) was mutated from 5 places became reliable only after it was rewritten as a single-consumer loop over a command channel.

questions.promptHtml: When is ConcurrentHashMap enough in coroutine code, and where does it still allow races? What about Collections.synchronizedList and CopyOnWriteArrayList?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: "Use a concurrent collection" is the standard answer, but most real bugs happen in compound operations. They want to know whether you see that.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: ConcurrentHashMap makes each single operation atomic and visible (get, put, putIfAbsent, compute, merge).
