It's enough when my logic is one operation per entry, like counting with merge or compute. It breaks the moment I compose operations: if (!map.containsKey(k)) map[k] = v is check-then-act, and two threads can both pass the check. I use the atomic compound methods (computeIfAbsent, putIfAbsent, compute, merge) instead. Also, iteration is weakly consistent: it won't throw ConcurrentModificationException but may or may not show concurrent changes. And it can't hold a suspend call: computeIfAbsent's lambda must be short, non-suspending and must not modify the map.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Collection Atomic unit Use when Watch out
ConcurrentHashMap Single op, per-bucket locking/CAS Shared caches, counters, registries No null keys or values (NPE); compound logic needs compute*/merge
Collections.synchronizedMap/List Each method call Quick wrap of a legacy collection Iteration still needs manual synchronized(list); compounds race
CopyOnWriteArrayList Whole-array copy per write Listeners/observers: many reads, rare writes O(n) per write; bad for frequent mutation
ConcurrentLinkedQueue Lock-free queue ops Producer/consumer without suspension No backpressure
Kotlin mutableMapOf() (LinkedHashMap) None Confined state only Not thread-safe at all

Kotlin-specific traps:

  • map.getOrPut(k) { v } on a ConcurrentMap has a JVM-friendly extension (ConcurrentMap.getOrPut) that uses putIfAbsent, so the value lambda can run more than once and the loser's value is discarded. For a plain MutableMap it is a check-then-act. If creation is expensive (a network call), neither is right.
  • Kotlin's map[k] = (map[k] ?: 0) + 1 is get-then-put and loses increments. map.merge(k, 1, Int::plus) is atomic (a Java 8 default method; API 24+ on Android, though ConcurrentHashMap has had its own merge/compute since API 24 too; below that, use a CAS loop with replace(k, old, new)).
  • computeIfAbsent with a blocking or long lambda locks that bin. Never do I/O there. Because it's not a suspend lambda, you can't suspend inside it anyway.

Which makes this the standard pattern for "fetch each key once": store a Deferred in the map and let the first caller start the fetch (see Q443).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val hits = ConcurrentHashMap<String, Int>()

fun recordBroken(k: String) { hits[k] = (hits[k] ?: 0) + 1 }          // lost increments
fun record(k: String) { hits.merge(k, 1, Int::plus) }                 // atomic

val cache = ConcurrentHashMap<String, Config>()
fun configFor(k: String): Config =
    cache.computeIfAbsent(k) { buildConfigCpuOnly(it) }               // short, pure, no suspend, no map writes inside

// BROKEN: check-then-act
fun configBroken(k: String): Config {
    if (!cache.containsKey(k)) cache[k] = buildConfigCpuOnly(k)       // two builders can race
    return cache[k]!!
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrapping a plain HashMap access in the coroutine and hoping because "it's mostly on Main".
  • synchronizedList plus for (x in list) iteration without holding the lock → ConcurrentModificationException.
  • ConcurrentHashMap<String, String?>: null values throw NullPointerException.
  • Using CopyOnWriteArrayList for a list that is updated 100 times a second.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is ConcurrentHashMap.size exact? → It's an estimate under concurrent modification.
  2. Why can't I await() inside computeIfAbsent? → The lambda isn't suspend, and blocking inside it would block the bin and maybe the dispatcher thread. Store Deferreds and await outside.
  3. Alternative to a concurrent map for UI state? → An immutable map in a StateFlow updated with update {}; readers always see a consistent snapshot.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "use ConcurrentHashMap, it's thread-safe". A senior says "single operations only", names the atomic compound methods, notes the no-null rule and weak iteration, and moves expensive computation outside the lambda.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A session cache ConcurrentHashMap<UserId, Session> with containsKey+put produced duplicate Session objects, and two analytics "session_start" events per user at login time.

questions.subtopic: Races at suspension points on a single thread
questions.promptHtml: Is code on Dispatchers.Main immune to races? Give an example of a data race-like bug in a single-threaded coroutine and explain how you'd fix it.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: "It's all on Main, so it's safe" is the most dangerous assumption in Android coroutine code. Seniors know that atomicity breaks at every suspension point.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Main has no parallel data races on plain fields, because only one coroutine runs at a time. But coroutines interleave at every suspension point, so logical races (check-then-act with a suspend call in between) are fully possible. Example: if (!loading) { loading = true; val d = api.load(); ... loading = false } is safe, since the check and the set happen with no suspension between them. But if (cache == null) { cache = api.load() } lets 10 callers all see null before the first load finishes, so there are 10 network calls and the last write wins. Fix: remove the gap between check and claim (set a flag or store a Deferred before suspending), or serialize with a Mutex.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Two different kinds of "race":

Kind Cause Happens on Main?
Data race (JMM) Unsynchronized concurrent memory access from several threads No (single thread)
Race condition (logic) Invariant broken by interleaving at suspension points Yes

The mental model: every suspension point is a place where all other coroutines on that thread may run. Between val a = x and x = a + 1 there is no gap if neither line suspends. If there's delay(), await(), withContext() or emit() in between, there is a gap.

Main thread timeline:
C1: read cache==null ── api.load() suspends ─────────────────────── cache = r1
C2:                      read cache==null ── api.load() suspends ───────────── cache = r2

Also dangerous on Main: emit() to a SharedFlow with a slow collector suspends, StateFlow.value reads that become stale across a suspension, and Mutex-less "optimistic UI" updates that roll back using a snapshot taken before the suspension.

Fix patterns, in order of preference:

  1. Claim before suspend: make the "decision" step synchronous, e.g. if (inFlight != null) return inFlight; inFlight = async { ... }. No suspension between check and claim, so on Main this is atomic.
  2. Re-check after suspend: after the suspend call, re-read state and decide again (if (cache == null) cache = r), or use update {}.
  3. Mutex around the whole sequence when ordering matters.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class ProfileVm(private val api: Api) : ViewModel() {
    private var cache: Profile? = null

    suspend fun profileBroken(): Profile {
        cache?.let { return it }
        val p = api.load()                  // suspension: other callers pass the null check meanwhile
        cache = p
        return p
    }

    private var inFlight: Deferred<Profile>? = null
    fun profile(): Deferred<Profile> =
        inFlight ?: viewModelScope.async { api.load() }.also { inFlight = it }   // claim is synchronous on Main
}

The profile() version is only race-free if all callers are on one thread. If callers can be on several threads, use a Mutex or a ConcurrentHashMap/compute for the claim.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using Dispatchers.Main.immediate and assuming "immediate" means no interleaving. It only skips a re-dispatch when you're already on Main; suspension points are still gaps.
  • Optimistic update: val old = state.value; state.value = optimistic; try { api() } catch { state.value = old } loses any updates that arrived during the call.
  • Treating isLoading guards as a lock without making the check and set adjacent.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does Dispatchers.Unconfined change anything? → Yes, it removes even the one-thread guarantee. Resumption runs on whichever thread resumes it, so data races are back.
  2. How would you test it? → In runTest with StandardTestDispatcher, launch two calls before advancing, then assert the API was hit once. The virtual scheduler shows the interleaving deterministically.
  3. Is the optimistic-update rollback fixable? → Roll back by reverse-applying only the failed change with update { } (e.g. remove that item), not by restoring a snapshot.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "Main is single-threaded so it's safe". A senior distinguishes data races from logic races, points to suspension points as the interleaving boundary, and fixes with claim-before-suspend, re-check, or Mutex.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "load profile if not cached" function called from 4 observers fired 4 identical requests on every cold start. That roughly quadrupled traffic on a hot endpoint, and nobody could see it in the single-threaded debugger.

questions.contextHtml:
A fintech app has 1.2M DAU. Access tokens live for 15 minutes. After a release that moved from Retrofit callbacks to coroutines, the support team reports random logouts: about 0.8% of sessions per day end with "Session expired, please log in again". Backend logs show that for those users, within 300 ms, there were 4 to 9 calls to POST /auth/refresh using the same refresh token. The first returned 200, and the rest returned 401 refresh_token_reused, which the server treats as theft and revokes the whole token family. The app code:

class AuthInterceptor(private val tokens: TokenStore, private val authApi: AuthApi) : Authenticator {
    override fun authenticate(route: Route?, response: Response): Request? {
        val refreshed = runBlocking {
            val r = authApi.refresh(tokens.refreshToken())
            tokens.save(r.access, r.refresh)
            r.access
        }
        return response.request.newBuilder().header("Authorization", "Bearer $refreshed").build()
    }
}

A home screen load fires 7 parallel requests. The token expires just before it loads. Red herrings: clocks on devices are off by a few seconds, and "this only started after the coroutines migration".
questions.promptHtml: Find the cause, fix it in a way that holds up under N parallel 401s, and describe what you'd do about the users already logged out.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add synchronized to authenticate" without noticing that other threads still send the stale token and then refresh again after the first refresh completes. Or "add a retry on the refresh call", which makes the reuse worse. Or blames the server.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the server rotate refresh tokens on every use (it seems so, given the reuse detection)? That makes the refresh single-use, which is the whole constraint. Is the refresh call made by OkHttp's Authenticator on its dispatcher threads, or by our own code? How many requests run in parallel at the home screen (7)? Is there any multi-process use (a widget or WorkManager) that could also refresh? Did the callbacks version have a lock we dropped?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ask the backend to relax reuse detection to a short grace window (e.g. accept the same refresh token for 10 s and return the same result) as a stop-gap. Roll the app back or hotfix the client behind a remote flag. Stop the forced logouts first because users are being locked out.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) No single-flight: each of the 7 failing calls refreshes independently. (b) A lock exists but doesn't check whether the token was already refreshed by the time the lock is acquired, so each waiter refreshes serially. (c) The refresh request itself goes through the same interceptor and gets a 401 loop. (d) Two processes. (a) and (b) fit the "4 to 9 calls in 300 ms" pattern.
  4. How I'd verify each: Add a request id and thread name to a debug log in authenticate. Reproduce with a test: MockWebServer that returns 401 for the old token and 200 for the new one, fire 10 parallel calls, and count refresh hits. The server logs already give the count. Confirm the pre-migration code held a lock by diffing history.
  5. Root cause: authenticate runs on up to N OkHttp dispatcher threads concurrently. Each calls refresh with the same refresh token because there is no mutual exclusion and no "was it already refreshed?" check. The first wins; the rest present a consumed token. Even adding a plain lock isn't enough: waiters acquire it one after another and each refreshes again using the new refresh token, burning one rotation per request.
  6. Fix: Single-flight refresh, with a stale-token check inside the lock. Compare against the access token that the failed request used:
class TokenRefresher(private val tokens: TokenStore, private val authApi: AuthApi) {
    private val mutex = Mutex()

    suspend fun refreshIfNeeded(failedAccessToken: String): String? = mutex.withLock {
        val current = tokens.accessToken()
        if (current != failedAccessToken) return current        // someone already refreshed; reuse it
        try {
            val r = authApi.refresh(tokens.refreshToken())
            tokens.save(r.access, r.refresh)
            r.access
        } catch (e: HttpException) {
            if (e.code() == 401) { tokens.clear(); null } else throw e   // 401: truly logged out
        }
    }
}

class AuthAuthenticator(private val refresher: TokenRefresher) : Authenticator {
    override fun authenticate(route: Route?, response: Response): Request? {
        val used = response.request.header("Authorization")?.removePrefix("Bearer ") ?: return null
        if (response.priorResponse != null) return null           // already retried once: give up (avoid loops)
        val fresh = runBlocking { refresher.refreshIfNeeded(used) } ?: return null
        return response.request.newBuilder().header("Authorization", "Bearer $fresh").build()
    }
}

runBlocking here is acceptable because OkHttp's Authenticator.authenticate is a blocking API called on an OkHttp thread, never the main thread. It does block that thread, which is why the refresh needs a timeout (OkHttp's call timeout applies to the refresh call, too). Mutex handles the "N waiters" case: the first refreshes, and the other six wake up, see current != failedAccessToken, and return the new token without any network call. The long-term options are a proactive refresh before expiry (a scheduled refresh at 80% of lifetime, guarded by the same mutex) and, if the backend allows it, a grace window as a safety net. Also persist tokens atomically (DataStore/EncryptedSharedPreferences write of both tokens in one commit) so a crash can't save an access token without its matching refresh token. 7. Prevention: A MockWebServer test with 20 parallel requests and exactly one /refresh hit expected. A metric refresh_calls_per_session with an alert. A review rule: any rotation of single-use credentials goes through one single-flight component. A chaos test with an expired token at startup. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not use synchronized with a boolean isRefreshing flag and let other requests proceed with the stale token, since they would fail with 401 anyway. I would not retry the refresh on 401 blindly, since a reused token revokes the family. I would not use a global Mutex in a multi-process app without also considering process boundaries; there I'd need a cross-process lock (file lock, or do the refresh in one process). A Mutex also means a slow refresh (say a 10 s timeout) blocks all calls behind it, which is acceptable because they cannot succeed anyway.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The refresh call itself times out after 10 s. What happens to the six waiters? → They wait for the lock one at a time. After the first fails (throws), the next acquires, sees the token unchanged, and tries again. That would be 6 sequential 10 s waits. I'd cache the failure for a short window (store a failed Deferred/timestamp) so waiters fail fast together.
  • A widget in another process also refreshes. → A process-local Mutex can't help. Either send refresh via a bound service or ContentProvider in the main process, or use a file lock plus re-reading the token from storage after acquiring it.
  • Can I do this with a Deferred instead of a Mutex? → Yes. Keep a @Volatile/atomic Deferred<String>? for the in-flight refresh; the first caller creates it and the rest await() it. Same single-flight idea, but all waiters share the same result and the same failure.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite of a payments app where a "harmless" refactor to parallel startup calls tripled refresh traffic. The first sign wasn't a crash but a 0.7% rise in logouts and a support spike on Monday. The fix was 25 lines. The test that would have caught it took an hour to write after the fact.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds a lock around the existing refresh call, and doesn't see that serial waiters still each refresh. No test plan.
  • Hire: Single-flight with Mutex or Deferred, stale-token comparison, bounded retry, MockWebServer concurrency test.
  • Strong hire: All of the above, plus the single-use rotation constraint, the timeout/failure fan-out for waiters, multi-process issues, atomic token persistence, proactive refresh and the backend-side mitigation.

questions.contextHtml:
A food-delivery app (400k orders per day) has a "Place order" button. Support finds 0.3% of orders (about 1,200 per day) are duplicated, and customers are charged twice. Server logs show pairs of POST /orders 40 to 150 ms apart with different request ids. The handler:

fun onPlaceOrderClicked() {
    viewModelScope.launch {
        _ui.value = _ui.value.copy(submitting = true)
        val result = orderRepo.placeOrder(cart)        // 600 ms to 3 s on poor networks
        _ui.value = _ui.value.copy(submitting = false, done = result.isSuccess)
    }
}

The button is disabled in the UI when submitting == true, which is collected with collectAsStateWithLifecycle. Red herrings: "Compose recomposes slowly", and a backend retry layer that is blamed first. The duplicates are mostly on low-end devices.
questions.promptHtml: Explain how two requests happen, fix it so it can't happen, and say what else you'd do beyond the client.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Disable the button after click." That is the existing mitigation, and it is exactly what fails: disabling depends on state propagating through StateFlow, then to composition, then to the next frame. A second tap can arrive before that. The weak answer also ignores server-side idempotency.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are the two requests from the same app process? (Request ids differ, so the app made two.) Do duplicates cluster on slow devices? (Yes, a longer UI delay gives a wider window.) Does the server support idempotency keys? Are we on Main in onPlaceOrderClicked? What is the timeline between taps (40-150 ms)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a client guard in a hotfix and, in parallel, have the backend dedupe by (userId, cartId) within a short window as a stop-gap. Refund the affected customers.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The UI disabled-state lags the click: two clicks are dispatched before the submitting=true recomposition removes the click handler. (b) The ViewModel launches a new coroutine for each call with no guard. (c) The user backgrounds and re-opens the app and the screen submits again. (d) An OkHttp automatic retry on connection failure (retryOnConnectionFailure). Timeline of 40-150 ms with different request ids points to (a) + (b).
  4. How I'd verify each: Log click timestamps and the thread in debug. Reproduce with a UI test that performs two performClick() calls back to back. Check request ids and User-Agent for OkHttp retry (the retry would keep the same request body but go through the same Call, so it would not show two different request ids at the server if you attach the id per Call). Check Crashlytics custom logs for double invocations.
  5. Root cause: The only guard is in the UI layer, which is asynchronous with respect to the click. The ViewModel function is not idempotent: two clicks run it twice. On Main each launch body runs until its first suspension, placeOrder, so both coroutines pass through submitting = true and both start a network call.
  6. Fix: Make the guard synchronous, and in the ViewModel, where the truth is. The claim happens before any suspension, so on Main it is atomic:
private var submitJob: Job? = null

fun onPlaceOrderClicked() {
    if (submitJob?.isActive == true) return                 // synchronous claim: second tap is dropped
    submitJob = viewModelScope.launch {
        _ui.update { it.copy(submitting = true) }
        val result = orderRepo.placeOrder(cart, idempotencyKey = checkoutId)   // same key for retries
        _ui.update { it.copy(submitting = false, done = result.isSuccess) }
    }
}

checkoutId is generated when the checkout screen is created (and saved in SavedStateHandle), not per click, so every retry of this order carries the same Idempotency-Key header and the server returns the original order. If the ViewModel can be invoked from several threads, use AtomicBoolean.compareAndSet(false, true) instead of the Job check. Also use _ui.update, since this is state touched by more than one writer. And if the job fails, reset the flag in finally. 7. Prevention: A UI test with a double click that asserts one request. A unit test with runTest: call onPlaceOrderClicked() twice before advancing time and assert that the fake repo is called once. Metrics for "orders with same cart within 5 s". Make the server contract require idempotency keys for all money-moving endpoints. A lint/review rule that every non-idempotent action has a synchronous in-flight guard. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not use debounce or throttleFirst on clicks alone. It narrows the window but doesn't close it (a retry after 1 s still doubles), and it makes the UI feel laggy. I would not use a Mutex here. A mutex would queue the second submit and run it after the first, which makes the duplicate order happen anyway; I want to drop it. I would not trust the UI state as the only guard.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The user taps, the request times out, and they tap again after 30 s. Is that a duplicate? → The first request may have succeeded on the server. The idempotency key (stable per checkout) lets the server return the same order. Without it, I would show "check your orders" instead of re-submitting blindly.
  • Process death during the request? → Persist checkoutId and "submit in flight" in SavedStateHandle/DB, and reconcile with the server on restart by querying the order by key.
  • What if the second tap should cancel the first and re-send? → Use a Job and cancel() then relaunch, but cancelling the coroutine does not undo a request the server already processed, so the idempotency key still matters.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite of a ticketing app: the team fixed double charges three times in the UI before the incident review asked "why can the server accept the same intent twice?" The idempotency key took one sprint and ended the whole class of bugs, including network-retry duplicates the UI fix could never touch.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Disables the button or adds a delay. No server angle.
  • Hire: Synchronous ViewModel guard (Job or Atomic flag), update, a test that double-invokes the function.
  • Strong hire: Idempotency key stability and persistence, explains why UI state lags, why Mutex is the wrong tool, process death, and cross-layer prevention.

questions.contextHtml:
A news app caches article details. After a refactor, the backend team reports that opening a feed with 30 visible cards triggers up to 90 requests for the same 30 article ids at once, and sometimes the UI shows the wrong article body in a card. Code:

class ArticleCache(private val api: ArticleApi) {
    private val cache = HashMap<String, Article>()
    private val confined = Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1)

    suspend fun get(id: String): Article = withContext(confined) {
        cache[id] ?: api.fetch(id).also { cache[id] = it }
    }

    suspend fun getIO(id: String): Article = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
        cache.getOrPut(id) { runBlocking { api.fetch(id) } }
    }
}

Cards call get(id), a prefetcher calls getIO(id). Crash logs sometimes show ConcurrentModificationException in HashMap.resize. Red herring: "Retrofit is not thread-safe" (it is).
questions.promptHtml: List every bug in this code, explain each mechanically, and rewrite it so each id is fetched at most once concurrently.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Replace HashMap with ConcurrentHashMap" and stop. That removes the corruption but not the duplicate fetches, and runBlocking stays. Another weak answer: "limitedParallelism(1) is a mutex so get is fine".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Should failed fetches be cached? Should a cancelled caller (a card scrolled off-screen) cancel the shared fetch? What is the eviction policy? Are the Article objects immutable? Does the ViewModel or the app own the cache's lifetime?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop the request storm with a quick client-side guard (de-dup in flight) and ask the backend for temporary rate-limit relief. The corruption (ConcurrentModificationException, wrong body) is a correctness bug, so it has to go in the same hotfix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) Check-then-act across a suspension in get: limitedParallelism(1) doesn't hold across api.fetch, so 3 cards for the same id all miss and all fetch. (2) getIO mutates the same HashMap from IO threads while get mutates it from the confined view: two different threads, no synchronization, so a data race and HashMap.resize corruption (this is where wrong bodies and the CME come from). (3) runBlocking inside withContext(Dispatchers.IO) blocks an IO thread per fetch; with the prefetcher it can exhaust the 64-thread IO pool. (4) getOrPut on a plain HashMap isn't atomic, either.
  4. How I'd verify each: A runTest-style test (with a real dispatcher for race checks) calling get("a") 20 times concurrently and counting api.fetch calls with a fake API. A stress test with 8 coroutines on Dispatchers.Default mixing get/getIO and asserting consistency. Thread dump or DebugProbes to see IO threads in runBlocking. StrictMode/Choreographer irrelevant here.
  5. Root cause: Two independent problems. (a) Confinement was broken by a second access path (getIO), so the "no lock needed" assumption fails. (b) Even in one path, the cache has a check-then-act with a suspend call in between, so it cannot de-duplicate. Confinement protects the map's memory, not the compound operation.
  6. Fix: One access path. Store in-flight Deferreds so the first caller starts the work and the rest await it. Claim the key synchronously under the confinement, and run the fetch outside:
class ArticleCache(private val api: ArticleApi, private val scope: CoroutineScope) {
    private val confined = Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1)
    private val inFlight = HashMap<String, Deferred<Article>>()      // touched only on `confined`

    suspend fun get(id: String): Article {
        val deferred = withContext(confined) {
            inFlight.getOrPut(id) {                                  // no suspension between check and put
                scope.async { api.fetch(id) }                        // runs in the cache's scope, not the caller's
            }
        }
        return try {
            deferred.await()
        } catch (e: Exception) {
            if (e is CancellationException && !deferred.isCancelled) throw e   // caller cancelled, keep the fetch
            withContext(confined) { inFlight.remove(id, deferred) }  // drop failed entries so they can retry
            throw e
        }
    }
}

Notes: withContext(confined) only executes the lambda that doesn't suspend, which is why the claim is atomic. The fetch runs in scope.async so one card scrolling away (cancelling its caller) does not cancel the fetch other cards wait for. Successful Deferreds stay in the map as the cache. For the bigger version, bound the size (an LRU) and expire entries. An alternative with fewer moving parts is ConcurrentHashMap<String, Deferred<Article>> plus computeIfAbsent { scope.async(start = CoroutineStart.LAZY) { ... } } then .await(), since LAZY deferred creation is cheap and the actual work starts on first await. 7. Prevention: The concurrency stress test above in CI on a real multi-thread dispatcher, repeated 1,000 times. A review rule: "one owner per mutable structure, one access path". An alert on request count per unique article id per minute. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not hold a Mutex around the fetch (it serializes all 30 different ids, taking 30x as long). I would not runBlocking in getIO. I would not cache failures forever. A cache scope tied to the Application means entries outlive screens, so memory must be bounded.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The fetch throws for one id. What do the 3 waiters see? → All three get the same exception from await(), then the entry is removed so the next call retries.
  • Why scope.async and not async in the caller? → An async started in the first caller's scope would be cancelled with that caller, failing the other waiters with a CancellationException they didn't cause.
  • Memory growth over a long session? → Replace the map with an LRU (LinkedHashMap with access order, or LruCache) behind the same confined access, and drop completed entries after storing results in a separate Article map.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite of an e-commerce app whose product cache "deduplicated" fine in tests on a single-thread test dispatcher. In production, the prefetch path added a second thread, and a monthly crash appeared as HashMap loops and wrong prices on cards. The post-mortem rule was "if state has an owner, nothing else touches it".

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Swaps in ConcurrentHashMap only, or thinks limitedParallelism(1) is a mutex.
  • Hire: Finds both the second thread access and the check-then-act across a suspension, fixes with in-flight Deferreds and a single access path.
  • Strong hire: Also covers scope ownership of the shared fetch, cancellation of one waiter, failure eviction, runBlocking starvation, LRU bounds, and a real-thread stress test.

questions.contextHtml: A photo backup feature uploads up to 2,000 photos. First version: photos.forEach { launch { api.upload(it) } } inside a coroutineScope. On mid-range devices (3 GB RAM) the app crashes with OOM at about 300 photos in flight, the server returns 429 for 35% of calls, and battery drain complaints rise. Each photo is read as a ~4 MB byte array before upload. A colleague suggests Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(3). After that change the OOM is still there and 429s drop only slightly. A trace shows 2,000 coroutines created and ~300 uploads active at once.
questions.promptHtml: Why didn't the colleague's change work? Design the bounded upload with correct failure and cancellation behavior.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "IO has 64 threads so it caps at 64" or "limitedParallelism(3) should limit it to 3". It misses that coroutines waiting on network don't hold a thread, so the thread limit does not limit in-flight requests. It also doesn't address the memory of loading bytes before the permit.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does the server allow per client (the 429s say there's a limit)? Is order important? Does one failure abort the batch? Can uploads resume after the app is killed (that points to WorkManager)? Is the byte array read before or after the limit?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap concurrency to 3 and read the file inside the permit (streaming through RequestBody, not a byte array). Ship with a remote config for the limit.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) The thread cap does not limit suspended coroutines, so 2,000 coroutines are created and all start their requests (OkHttp queues beyond its own limits but the byte arrays were already created). (2) Reading the bytes before acquiring any limit multiplies memory. (3) OkHttp's dispatcher defaults (64 total, 5 per host) apply, so many calls sit queued in OkHttp holding their memory.
  4. How I'd verify each: Android Studio memory profiler heap dump (count of byte[] ≥ 4 MB), coroutine count via debug probes or a counter, OkHttp EventListener logging queued calls, server-side logs for concurrency per user.
  5. Root cause: limitedParallelism(n) restricts threads executing code, not coroutines in flight. A coroutine suspended on await of a network call isn't using a thread, so the slot is free for another to start, and 300 uploads proceed. The right limit is on in-flight operations: a Semaphore, a bounded worker pool, or flatMapMerge.
  6. Fix: Semaphore with the permit around both reading and sending, and fail-fast or collect failures deliberately:
suspend fun backup(photos: List<Photo>): BackupResult = coroutineScope {
    val permits = Semaphore(3)
    val results = photos.map { p ->
        async(Dispatchers.IO) {
            permits.withPermit {                                   // read AND upload under the permit
                runCatching { api.upload(p.uri.openStream().asRequestBody()) }
                    .onFailure { if (it is CancellationException) throw it }
            }
        }
    }.awaitAll()
    BackupResult(ok = results.count { it.isSuccess }, failed = results.count { it.isFailure })
}

Still creates 2,000 lightweight coroutines (about a few hundred bytes each: cheap), but only 3 hold memory. For very large lists, consume a Channel/asFlow().flatMapMerge(3) { flow { emit(upload(it)) } } with no per-item coroutine. The runCatching rethrows CancellationException so cancelling the batch cancels waiting items. Retry with backoff for 429 (honor Retry-After), and for a real backup feature, run it in a CoroutineWorker with a foreground service so the OS doesn't kill it. 7. Prevention: A test with a fake API that tracks max concurrent calls and asserts <= 3. A memory budget test on a low-RAM emulator. A review checklist item: "what bounds work in flight, and is it bounded before allocation?". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not use Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(3) as the fix. It also limits unrelated work sharing that view, and is the wrong abstraction. I would not set the permit count to 64 because "IO has 64". The right number comes from server limits, radio behavior and memory: roughly 3-4.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• One upload hangs forever. → Wrap the upload in withTimeout per item (and set OkHttp timeouts), release the permit via withPermit, and record a failure. A hung item must not hold a permit.
  • How do you show overall progress from parallel uploads? → An AtomicInteger/update {} on a StateFlow<Progress>; don't use var done++.
  • User cancels. → Cancelling the scope cancels waiting acquire() calls and in-flight OkHttp calls; verify with a test that no permit leaks.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite of a backup feature: the first fix capped threads and shipped; the OOM rate dropped only 10%. Reading the heap dump, 280 identical 4 MB arrays pointed at the real bug: allocation was happening before the limiter, not after.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Thinks the thread cap limits in-flight requests; doesn't address memory.
  • Hire: Semaphore (or flatMapMerge) with the work inside the permit, bounded concurrency test.
  • Strong hire: Explains threads vs in-flight coroutines, allocation placement, 429/Retry-After, cancellation and permit leaks, WorkManager for durability.

questions.contextHtml: You are designing the shared in-memory state for a messaging app's sync engine: (1) an unread counter updated by 3 sources (socket, push, DB triggers) at up to 200 updates/s in bursts, (2) a map of conversationId -> draft mutated by UI and a background saver, (3) an "outbox" queue where order matters and each send includes a network call (200 ms to 5 s), (4) a "last sync token" read by many and written rarely. A teammate proposes "one global Mutex for everything". Another proposes "make everything @Volatile".
questions.promptHtml: Pick a mechanism for each of the four, with reasons. Then say how you'd test the choices.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks one tool for all four. Both proposals fail: the global mutex serializes a 5 s network call behind counter increments; @Volatile fixes visibility only and leaves lost updates.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the unread counter need exactness or only eventual correctness (it could be derived from the DB)? Who reads each piece, and does the UI observe it? Must outbox order be strict per conversation or global? What happens on process death?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident, so I'd use this step to decide the ownership model: for each piece of state, one owner and one access path.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (candidate designs): (a) Atomics / StateFlow.update for independent single-value state; (b) confinement for state with many fields; (c) Actor/Channel for ordered, effectful work; (d) immutable snapshot with volatile publish for read-mostly values; (e) Mutex for rare multi-step suspend sections.
  4. How I'd verify each: Stress tests with real dispatchers; Lincheck-style tests if available; a load test at 5x the burst rate; Perfetto traces to look for contention and long critical sections.
  5. Root cause: n/a. The principle: match the primitive to the shape of the operation, not to the habit.
  6. Fix (my choices):
State Shape Choice Why
Unread counter One value, 200 updates/s, no suspension MutableStateFlow<Int> with update { it + 1 } (or AtomicInteger + flow) Lock-free CAS, UI can observe it, retries are cheap
Drafts map Compound structure, UI + saver, short CPU operations Immutable Map in MutableStateFlow with update { it + (id to text) }, saver reads snapshots Consistent snapshots for readers, no locks; copy cost fine for small maps (use persistent collections if large)
Outbox Ordered, effectful, long suspend calls Single-consumer loop over a Channel<OutgoingMessage> (actor-style), with per-conversation workers if parallelism is needed Order by construction; slow sends don't block other state; backpressure via channel capacity
Sync token Read-mostly scalar @Volatile var or AtomicReference<String>, written by the single sync coroutine Visibility is all that is needed with a single writer 
class SyncState {
    private val _unread = MutableStateFlow(0)
    val unread: StateFlow<Int> = _unread.asStateFlow()
    fun onNewMessage() = _unread.update { it + 1 }

    private val _drafts = MutableStateFlow<Map<String, String>>(emptyMap())
    fun setDraft(id: String, text: String) = _drafts.update { it + (id to text) }

    @Volatile var syncToken: String? = null          // single writer: the sync loop
        private set
}
  1. Prevention: Document the owner of each piece of state in the class KDoc. A code-review rule: no mutable collection escapes its owner. A stress test per structure.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): No global Mutex (it couples a 5 s network call to the counter, and any new feature creates lock-ordering risk). No @Volatile for compound updates. Not using an actor for the counter (needless overhead and latency). I'd note that update on _drafts copies the map on every write: fine for dozens of drafts, bad for 10,000. Then a confined mutable map with snapshots would be better.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The unread counter must match the DB exactly. → Don't increment in memory at all. Derive it from a Room COUNT Flow. The DB becomes the owner.
  • Burst goes 10x. → CAS contention grows; for pure counting use LongAdder-like striping, or conflate updates (batch every 100 ms) before touching state.
  • Outbox must run 4 sends in parallel but keep per-conversation order. → One channel per conversation (or sharded by conversationId.hashCode() % 4), each with one consumer.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite of a chat app where a single "StateLock" was added after a race; six months later it was held across a socket write and the whole UI froze whenever the radio stalled. The rewrite split state into independent owners and the freezes ended.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: One mechanism for everything.
  • Hire: Correct mechanism per case with a reason (atomic/update, snapshot, channel, volatile).
  • Strong hire: Ownership model, ordering vs parallelism, copy-cost caveats, DB-as-source-of-truth alternative, and test strategy for each.

questions.contextHtml:
A trading app's QuoteRepository protects its cache with one Mutex:

class QuoteRepository(private val api: QuoteApi, private val dao: QuoteDao) {
    private val mutex = Mutex()
    suspend fun quote(symbol: String): Quote = mutex.withLock {
        dao.get(symbol)?.takeIf { it.isFresh() } ?: api.fetch(symbol).also { dao.put(it) }
    }
}

At 50k DAU it was fine. After onboarding a partner (500k DAU) and adding a watchlist of 40 symbols per screen, the watchlist takes 8 to 25 s to render (p95), though the API p95 is 180 ms. There are no crashes; ANR rate is unchanged. A thread dump shows nothing blocked. The product team suspects the API.
questions.promptHtml: Why is it slow, how do you prove it, and what is the right structure?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the API timeout/scale the backend", or "switch the Mutex to synchronized", which would block threads and create ANRs or starvation instead.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the watchlist loaded with parallel async per symbol (40 callers)? What's the cache hit rate? Does the slowness appear only on cold cache or all the time? Is the same repository instance shared by many screens or users?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Turn on a remote flag to load the watchlist with a single batch endpoint if one exists, or raise cache freshness TTL temporarily to cut fetches.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) The Mutex serializes everything, including network I/O. 40 symbols x 180 ms = 7.2 s, with retries and slower tails it reaches 25 s; with several screens competing it is worse. (2) Slow API tail amplifies: one 5 s call blocks all other callers. (3) The DB is slow. (4) The backend is slow (contradicted by p95 180 ms).
  4. How I'd verify each: Log time-in-queue for mutex.lock() vs time-in-critical-section (timestamps around withLock entry and body). The numbers show queue wait ≈ 90% of latency. Perfetto custom trace sections (Trace.beginAsyncSection) show 40 calls as a staircase. DebugProbes dump shows many coroutines SUSPENDED in MutexImpl.lock. Thread dump is empty of blocked threads, which matches: suspending waiters don't block threads, so this problem doesn't look like a hang.
  5. Root cause: A global lock protecting I/O. The invariant to protect is "each symbol is fetched once and the cache stays consistent", not "only one fetch in the app at a time". The Mutex enforces the second, much stronger, condition. Throughput = 1 / (average critical-section time) ≈ 5 calls/s no matter how many cores or connections are available.
  6. Fix: Lock only the bookkeeping, not the I/O, and key the work per symbol (single-flight per key, as in Q443), so different symbols run in parallel and the same symbol is fetched once:
class QuoteRepository(private val api: QuoteApi, private val dao: QuoteDao, private val scope: CoroutineScope) {
    private val lock = Mutex()
    private val inFlight = HashMap<String, Deferred<Quote>>()     // guarded by `lock`

    suspend fun quote(symbol: String): Quote {
        dao.get(symbol)?.takeIf { it.isFresh() }?.let { return it }     // fast path, no lock
        val d = lock.withLock {                                          // short: no I/O inside
            inFlight.getOrPut(symbol) {
                scope.async { api.fetch(symbol).also { dao.put(it) } }
                    .also { job -> job.invokeOnCompletion { scope.launch { lock.withLock { inFlight.remove(symbol) } } } }
            }
        }
        return d.await()
    }
}

With 40 symbols the load time becomes about max(call time) ≈ 180-400 ms, or a bounded Semaphore(6) if the server rate-limits. Better still, batch: api.fetch(symbols) once. If the quote must be strictly consistent (a write requires exclusion), use a per-key Mutex map or striped locks rather than a global one. 7. Prevention: A load test with 40 concurrent callers and a fake API that has 200 ms latency: assert total time under 1 s. Metrics for lock wait time. A review rule: "no network or disk I/O inside a shared lock". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't replace the Mutex with synchronized because that blocks threads and risks starving Default/IO. I wouldn't drop locking entirely, since that reintroduces duplicate fetches. Per-key maps add memory and removal complexity (hence the invokeOnCompletion cleanup), so I'd keep the code in one class with a test.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• How does this look in a Perfetto trace compared with a blocked thread? → There's no long slice on any thread. Work is just absent: gaps between small network slices. That is why the thread dump showed nothing.
  • Tail latency: one symbol hangs. → Per-key means only that symbol waits. Add withTimeout per fetch and serve stale cache on failure.
  • 10x more users? → Backend and radio become the bottleneck, so rely on server batch, push updates over a socket, and an HTTP cache.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite of a pricing screen: the team scaled backend pods twice before someone plotted lock wait time. The fix was twelve lines and a unit test with a 200 ms fake, and dropped screen load from 14 s to 0.4 s.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames the API or backend; swaps to synchronized.
  • Hire: Spots lock-over-I/O, proves with lock wait metrics, moves I/O outside the lock.
  • Strong hire: Per-key single-flight, bounded concurrency, explains why thread dumps look clean, load test design, batch endpoint and stale-on-failure.

questions.subtopic: Legacy callback threads sharing state with coroutines
questions.contextHtml: A video-conferencing app is migrating its call manager from Java to Kotlin coroutines, one class at a time. The vendor SDK (Java, closed source) delivers onParticipantJoined/Left callbacks on its own 2 internal threads. The new Kotlin CallViewModel keeps participants: MutableList<Participant>, mutated by the SDK callbacks and read by a coroutine on Main that builds the UI state. Crash reports after the rollout to 10% of traffic: 0.6% of calls crash with ConcurrentModificationException, and 0.2% show a participant tile for someone who already left. A teammate wrapped the callback bodies in mutex.withLock via runBlocking, and ANR rate went from 0.1% to 0.9% on that cohort.
questions.promptHtml: Design the safe boundary between the SDK callbacks and the coroutine world, and explain what went wrong in the runBlocking attempt.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use CopyOnWriteArrayList" (fixes the CME but not the stale ordering between join/leave events), or "keep runBlocking, just increase timeouts".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the SDK guarantee callback order per participant? Which thread delivers the callbacks, and is it safe to block them (the SDK may time out if callbacks are slow)? How frequent are events (in a 50-person call maybe 5 to 20 per second at join storms)? Does the UI need every event or only the latest participant set?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Halt the rollout (or turn the feature flag off for the cohort), because ANR and crash increases are user-visible. Revert the runBlocking change first, since it is the worse of the two.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) The mutable list is mutated on SDK threads and read on Main with no synchronization: CME and a torn view. (2) Event ordering across the two SDK threads isn't preserved (join and leave for one person processed out of order → stale tile). (3) runBlocking inside SDK callbacks blocks SDK threads and, when the Mutex is held by a Main-thread coroutine that is waiting for the SDK, it creates a cross-thread wait cycle → ANR. (4) UI snapshot built from a list while it changes.
  4. How I'd verify each: Crashlytics stack traces (the CME is thrown at the iteration on Main). ANR traces: SDK thread blocked in runBlocking → BlockingCoroutine.joinBlocking; Main in Mutex.lock's coroutine waiting. A replay test that fires join/leave events from 2 threads at 1 kHz while collecting UI state. Check the SDK docs about threading and ordering.
  5. Root cause: The boundary was left implicit. Two threads and Main touch the same mutable list, and the "fix" brought blocking into a callback thread and re-entered the coroutine world with runBlocking, which ties an SDK thread's liveness to a coroutine Mutex that Main coroutines also need.
  6. Fix: Make the callbacks do nothing but hand off, then process in one place:
class CallEvents {
    private val inbox = Channel<ParticipantEvent>(Channel.UNLIMITED)   // trySend never blocks the SDK thread

    // SDK thread: non-blocking, thread-safe hand-off
    fun onJoined(p: Participant) { inbox.trySend(ParticipantEvent.Joined(p)) }
    fun onLeft(id: String) { inbox.trySend(ParticipantEvent.Left(id)) }

    val participants: Flow<List<Participant>> = flow {
        var current = persistentListOf<Participant>()                 // owned by this one collector coroutine
        for (e in inbox) {
            current = when (e) {
                is ParticipantEvent.Joined -> current.add(e.p)
                is ParticipantEvent.Left -> current.removeAll { it.id == e.id }
            }
            emit(current)                                             // immutable snapshot
        }
    }
}

Channel.trySend is non-blocking and thread-safe, so SDK threads return immediately and the single consumer processes events in arrival order. State has one owner (the collecting coroutine), the UI receives immutable snapshots, and there is no lock. To keep strict order across the SDK's two threads, assign a sequence number if the SDK provides one; if the SDK does not guarantee ordering, I would reconcile by asking the SDK for the full participant list on each event (the source of truth), rather than trusting the deltas. UNLIMITED is safe here because events are tiny and bounded by call size, but I'd add a drop-oldest+resync policy for a bound. For a flow, callbackFlow with trySend is the equivalent ready-made form (C10 chunk). 7. Prevention: Rule: "SDK callbacks may only trySend/post". A stress test replaying shuffled join/leave events from two threads. Lint/review: no runBlocking outside main() and tests. ANR monitoring per cohort in the staged rollout. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I'd not use CopyOnWriteArrayList as the sole fix since the ordering bug remains. I'd not runBlocking in callbacks (blocks SDK threads, cycle risk). I'd not marshal each event to Main with Handler.post and mutate there if Main is already busy; the channel consumer can run on Default and only the final state goes to Main. A single consumer adds a tiny latency per event, which is acceptable for join/leave.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the SDK requires the callback to return a value computed from our state? → Then keep a lock-free read model for that answer (a volatile reference to the latest immutable snapshot) so the callback reads it without suspending.
  • Events arrive at 5k/s in a bad network (reconnect storm). → Conflate by participant id before applying (keep the last event per id) or resync from the SDK's list; don't let the channel grow unbounded.
  • Why not just a Mutex with tryLock() in callbacks? → It drops events when contended, so state is silently wrong.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite of a conferencing migration: the team's first two fixes (a lock, then runBlocking) each made the dashboard look worse. The third attempt drew the thread boundary on a whiteboard first, and the diff was smaller than either earlier fix.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Wraps the list in a concurrent collection or uses runBlocking in callbacks.
  • Hire: Non-blocking hand-off (channel/callbackFlow), single owner of state, immutable snapshots.
  • Strong hire: Explains the ANR cycle mechanically, event ordering and resync strategy, bounded/conflated buffering, staged rollout metrics, and the "callbacks only post" rule.
